_README: Approach variants — CASCADE PASS / ELDORADO core of the Washington North Cascades, 2026-08-19.
44 routes, 44 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Several ids in
this batch carry no peak name at all, and two of them are filed under an area whose own name is generic:
wa_tepeh_towers, wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete, wa_eldorado_peak_north_ridge and the rest of the Eldorado group all
sit under `wa_main_peak` — an area literally named 'Main Peak' beneath wa_eldorado_peak. wa_southeast_face is
SHARKFIN TOWER, wa_northwest_ridge is DORADO NEEDLE, wa_north_ridge_4 and wa_east_slope are PRIMUS PEAK,
wa_north_ridge_7 is AIGUILLE DE L'M, wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route is JOHANNESBURG, and wa_mount_logan_r1 / r2 are
the Banded and Douglas glacier routes on MOUNT LOGAN. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which peak you are on.
SCOPE. The request named 23 peaks. 21 of them exist as areas in this catalog; Tepeh Towers exists only as a ROUTE
(wa_tepeh_towers, filed under wa_main_peak) and is covered here on that row. Two requested peaks have no Washington
row at all and could not be covered — see _SKIPPED for both, and note that BOTH carry a live name-collision risk.
Two areas beside the named peaks were included because the catalog files them inside the same Boston Basin subtree
and their routes were empty: wa_aiguille_de_l_m and wa_boston_basin (the latter holds no direct routes).
53 routes across those areas had an EMPTY approach_variants. 44 are written here and 9 were deliberately skipped.
12 routes in scope ALREADY had variants and were not touched — including wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge, which the
request explicitly protects, and wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge and wa_mount_torment_south_ridge, whose nulled
rappel lengths are recorded as settled and were not re-opened.
CONTAMINATION REJECTED, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- AIGUILLE DE L'M is the loudest one and it came out the other way. The famous Aiguille de l'M is in CHAMONIX,
FRANCE, and a Boston Basin area of that name reads instantly like an import error. It is not: Mountain Project
carries a Washington area at 48.50663, -121.06681 — which matches this catalog's area coordinate exactly — and
the American Alpine Institute has a route profile for its North Ridge. It is the cockscomb dividing the high
Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on one side, and it was named by a guide for the
resemblance. A deliberate echo, not a filing error. No Chamonix material was used for any field.
- MOUNTAIN PROJECT'S 'Chockstone Route' (route id 111959715) IS NORTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE AT WASHINGTON PASS,
not Austera Peak. Both are Washington, both are in this catalog, and both have a chockstone; that page must
never be used as a source for wa_austera_peak_chockstone_route. Caught and excluded during research.
- MOUNT LOGAN: the famous one is in the YUKON and is Canada's highest peak; there is another in Utah. Only the
9,087 ft North Cascades peak with the Douglas, Fremont and Banded glaciers was used.
- MOUNT GOODE: there is a 13,092 ft Mount Goode in the Sierra Nevada near Bishop, California. Only the 9,200 ft
peak above the North Fork of Bridge Creek was used.
- STORM KING: three near-misses were found and rejected — a Storm King in Colorado's San Juans (an 18-pitch 5.7,
FA Bliss/Jones 1974), Storm King Mountain in New York's Hudson Highlands, and MOUNT STORM KING in OLYMPIC
National Park above Lake Crescent. The tell for the North Cascades one is that it carries NO 'Mount' prefix.
- ELDORADO: 'West Arete' returned a Mountain Project page for ELDORADO CANYON STATE PARK, COLORADO. Excluded.
- MAGIC MOUNTAIN is also a ski area, an amusement park, a peak in Idaho and one in California. Only the 7,610 ft
Cascade Pass peak above Kool-Aid Lake and Pelton Basin was used.
- BOSTON PEAK and CASCADE PEAK are both generic names; every source used is anchored to Boston Basin, the Quien
Sabe Glacier or the Cascade-Johannesburg col.
NO TIME, DISTANCE OR GAIN FIGURE IS WRITTEN INTO ANY VARIANT except one `hours` on the Aiguille de l'M, where a
single source states a half day from Boston Basin camp and nothing contradicts it. Everything else was omitted:
the catalog states Eldorado's own summit three different ways (8,868 / 8,872 / 8,873 ft) across rows in the same
area, Goode's Northeast Buttress moat is published at anywhere from 6,400 to 7,800 ft depending on the year the
party went, and Dorado Needle's Southwest Buttress is 9 pitches at 5.8 in one source and 13 at 5.7 in another.
Where sources disagreed the disagreement is stated in prose rather than averaged into a number.
NO URL OR SOURCE NAME APPEARS IN ANY name / notes / baseFinding / hazards field. Sources are in `_sources` only.
Every URL in a _sources list was actually retrieved during this pass; nothing was pattern-guessed. Entries whose
material comes from the route row's OWN approach / climbing_route / descent_text prose carry an EMPTY _sources
and are labelled 're-homed'.
_confidence values: 'corroborated' (two or more independent retrieved sources, or one source plus the row's own
columns agreeing on the base), 'single-source' (one retrieved source), 're-homed' (material comes from the row's
own columns; nothing was researched into it and no source is claimed), and 'thin' (the base is real but
under-published — the entry says so inside its own baseFinding).

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier, then north to the foot of the ridge
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, for dry rock and a glacier that is still bridged where it matters
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft on Cascade River Road, the old Diamond Mine roadbed runs about a mile to the mine site, then the climbers' path climbs hard through forest with four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at about 6,400 ft.

From high camp, follow the moraine and the west edge of the QUIEN SABE GLACIER up to about 7,500 ft and climb to SHARKFIN COL at 7,720 ft — roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and 200 ft of a class 3 gully to gain it, on loose scree underfoot.

The col is the commitment. From it you make a rappel of roughly 150 ft down a loose gully onto the BOSTON GLACIER; retreat after that means re-climbing to the col. Traverse north through crevassed ground toward the north end of the glacier, then re-ascend to the ridge.

Three Forbidden routes cross Sharkfin Col and use this rappel. Where you LEAVE the Boston Glacier is what separates them, and that is what the baseFinding below is about.
hazards: A rappel of about 150 ft down a loose gully off the col, with rope-snag on loose rock, and no easy retreat once you are down it
A heavily crevassed traverse of the Boston Glacier where a fall would be serious
A distinct moat where the glacier meets the North Ridge rock, sometimes needing technical work to exit, and worse late season
Steep snow gully sections on the ridge itself where a slip runs uncontrolled onto the Boston Glacier
A long, exposed crest with the descent on a completely different side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FIRST, IDENTIFY SHARKFIN COL CORRECTLY, BECAUSE EVERYTHING AFTER IT IS COMMITTED. It is the LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE IMMEDIATELY LEFT OF SHARKFIN TOWER — a distinct rock tower stands beside it. A notch on that skyline with no tower beside it is not the col. You gain it by about 10 ft of 5.7 and a 200 ft class 3 gully; if you walked up to it, you are somewhere else.

SECOND, ON THE BOSTON GLACIER, GO NORTH AND KEEP GOING. The base of this route is at the FAR NORTH END of the glacier, where the ice meets the foot of the ridge, and the crossing point is itself a notch rather than an arbitrary spot on the crest. You should pass a rock buttress on the way; if you have turned uphill without passing it, you have turned too early.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THE FIRST MOVE, AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: THE CLIMBING STARTS WITH A SHORT, STEEP LEFT-FACING CORNER AT 5.6, STRAIGHT OFF THE COL AT THE FOOT OF THE RIDGE. That corner is the route's crux and it is the first thing you climb. IF THE FIRST GROUND ABOVE THE GLACIER IS 300 FT OF LOW-ANGLE ROCK LEADING TOWARD AN ICE PATCH, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHEAST FACE and you turned west off the glacier far too soon.

AND YOU SHOULD BE AT A COL, NOT ON A FACE. The base is the gap between Boston and Forbidden: ground falls away on BOTH sides of you. If the mountain is above you and glacier below you and nothing behind, you are under a face, not at the col.

CONFIRM AS YOU CLIMB: above the corner the crest passes a wildly exposed bivy platform — two small snow-free spots just below the crest on the northeast side — and above roughly 8,400 ft the rock notably improves. Poor rock all the way to the top means you never got onto the upper ridge.

approach_variants.name: East around the basin and up the loose gullies to the notch below the Solitary Gendarme
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; August is the most reliable for dry granite
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and Boston Basin climbers' trail as the West Ridge — the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about a mile, then a steep path with several creek crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft, then talus and heather to the usual high camp at 6,300-6,600 ft, roughly four to five miles and three to four hours from the car.

From camp, do NOT cross toward the south-face couloir. Traverse climber's-left and east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies flanking the glacier on Forbidden's east side, sometimes loosely called the Unnamed Glacier. This leg is the honest part of the route's reputation: a few hours over choss-covered slabs, loose rock and seepage, several small stream crossings, and usually a snow gully at the end that wants crampons or microspikes to gain the upper benches. Parties describe holding a bearing of roughly 058 degrees up the east side of that glacier.

Reckon five to six hours and over 5,000 ft above the trailhead to the notch — noticeably longer and far more route-finding than reaching the West Ridge notch.
hazards: Hours of loose, choss-covered slabs and seepage on the approach, with real route-finding in poor visibility
A snow gully at the top of the approach that wants crampons even in midsummer
Aging fixed rappel anchors in the gendarme notches
Sustained exposure and complex route-finding over multiple gendarmes once on the crest
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long crest with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LANDMARK IS A SINGLE TOWER WITH A NAME: THE SOLITARY GENDARME. The high bivy sits at roughly 8,000 ft, about 300 ft BELOW it, and the notch where the technical climbing starts is just above that bivy. A lone tower standing up on the crest, with the ridge running away west toward the summit, is the confirmation you are at the right place on a ridge that offers many wrong ones.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN ELSEWHERE: this crest carries several gendarmes and the ridge can be joined almost anywhere along it. Joining it high — past the gendarmes, with an unobstructed view of the summit and nothing in the way — means you have missed the route rather than found a shortcut. IF THERE IS NOTHING BETWEEN YOU AND THE SUMMIT, YOU ARE TOO HIGH.

THE FIRST MOVE TEST: from the notch you go LEFT around the first gendarme, then simul-climb easy blocks at about 5.4 on clean granite to gain the crest proper. Easy ground first, hard ground later. If your opening pitch is hard, you are not on the East Ridge Direct.

THE DIRECT LINE IS DEFINED BY REFUSING THE BYPASSES. Every gendarme here can be walked around on the north or south flank. A day that never once required a move you would rope up for means you have been taking the bypasses and are on the easier variant, not the Direct.

CONFIRM AT THE CRUX, LATE: the 5.8 crux comes after climbing a steep pitch up the LAST gendarme and RAPPELLING DOWN ITS BACK SIDE into a narrow notch with a steep wall directly ahead. A notch you scrambled into rather than rappelled into is not that notch.

DO NOT CONFUSE THIS RIDGE WITH THE EAST LEDGES. The Ledges are the loose descent traverse that stays WELL BELOW the crest and rejoins the ridge near the Solitary Gendarme. If you are traversing ledges rather than climbing a crest, you are on the descent line — the one that carries a documented fatality.

approach_variants.name: All the way round to the Forbidden Glacier's north arm
approach_variants.season: Mid summer, for the best balance of firm ice and dry rock
approach_variants.notes:
This is the hardest-to-reach established line on the peak and most parties treat it as three days.

The recorded approach goes the long way round: from the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft, often pushing on to a bench near 7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe to the notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse that heavily crevassed glacier, and continue around to the NORTH ARM OF THE FORBIDDEN GLACIER on the mountain's other side.

Other parties reach the same basin without the Boston Glacier at all — by dropping west off the North Ridge line, by rappelling from the West Ridge notch over crevasses and moats, or over Torment Col. All of them end in the same place, which is what the baseFinding uses.

From the north arm, about 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice leads to the base of the rock.
hazards: Two crevassed glaciers before any climbing, with a large crevasse that opens around 7,600 ft in many seasons and can cost real time
A committing rappel off Sharkfin Col — retreat means re-climbing to the col
A moat or bergschrund where the snow pulls back from the foot of the rib
A shaded, cold aspect that holds hard ice late, and a face that tops out at a cornice near 8,375 ft
A descent on a completely different side of the mountain, by the West Ridge couloir
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECIDING FACT IS WHICH GLACIER YOU ARE STANDING ON, AND IT SETTLES THIS ROUTE AGAINST BOTH ITS NEIGHBOURS IN ONE LOOK. This route starts from the FORBIDDEN GLACIER'S NORTH ARM, on the mountain's WEST side. The North Ridge and the Northeast Face both start from the BOSTON GLACIER, on the east. If your approach ended on the Boston Glacier and you started climbing there, you are on one of those two, not this.

THE POSITIVE LANDMARK IS THE RIB. From the north arm an obvious rock rib runs roughly 1,800 ft up the face, with ICE ON BOTH SIDES OF IT — the face is two ice sections split by a narrow rock band. You should be able to see a continuous rib rising from where you stand. IF WHAT IS ABOVE YOU IS A BROAD, UNDIFFERENTIATED SNOW AND ICE SLOPE WITH NO RIB IN IT, YOU ARE NOT UNDER THIS ROUTE.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS SNOW, NOT ROCK. Above the moat comes roughly 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice BEFORE any technical rock. If you stepped off the glacier straight onto rock, you are on the Northeast Face — which begins with 300 ft of rock and only then reaches its ice.

COUNT THE GROUND ABOVE THE ICE: about 500 ft of somewhat loose 4th to low-5th, soloed or simul-climbed, leads to a KNIFE-EDGE RIDGE crossed at 5.6, and the 5.8 crux follows immediately after it. A knife edge is the confirmation that you are on the rib and not on ground beside it.

AND THE LARGE CREVASSE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT IS A POSITION MARKER AS WELL AS A HAZARD — it opens on the approach in most seasons and is the thing most likely to make you detour; note where you crossed it, because you are not reversing this way.

approach_variants.name: Sharkfin Col, the schrund rappel and an ice wall, then west across the Boston Glacier to the ice patch
approach_variants.season: Late spring to early summer, when the face still holds the best ice and snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft. Continue along the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to SHARKFIN COL at about 7,720 ft, gained by roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and a class 3 gully.

The first-ascent party rappelled from the col INTO the bergschrund and climbed a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the Boston Glacier. Expect the schrund to be the awkward part of the day before the climbing starts.

From the glacier, traverse WEST — a short traverse, not the long northward one the North Ridge makes — to the base of the face.

This line is climbed rarely enough that no fixed gear should be assumed and modern first-hand descriptions are scarce; treat any description of it, including this one, as an outline.
hazards: A rappel into a bergschrund and a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the glacier
A north-facing ice feature that has thinned over recent decades — verify there is ice deep enough to take a screw rather than assuming it
Everything on the face funnels through the ice patch, so it is the exposed spot for anything released from above
A remote position with a long, complex retreat and a descent by the West Ridge on the far side of the peak
So few ascents that conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ICE PATCH IS THE LANDMARK AND YOUR POSITION RELATIVE TO IT IS THE WHOLE TEST. From the Boston Glacier a large, conspicuous patch of ice sits on the lower face — about 300 ft tall. YOU START ON ROCK BELOW AND TO THE LEFT (WEST) OF IT, NOT ON IT AND NOT TO ITS RIGHT.

SO THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS: ROCK FIRST, ICE SECOND. About 300 ft of rock, protected by a few pitons on the first ascent, comes before you reach the ice at all. IF YOU ARE SWINGING TOOLS WITHIN A ROPE-LENGTH OF LEAVING THE GLACIER, YOU HAVE STARTED TOO FAR RIGHT — you are on the patch itself rather than the rock beside it.

COUNT THE THREE SECTIONS IN ORDER: 300 ft of rock, then 300 ft of ice at about 50 degrees, then about 600 ft of steep-looking but upward-dipping slabs to the top. A route that stays on one medium the whole way is not this one.

TELL IT FROM THE NORTH RIDGE BY HOW FAR YOU WALKED. Both cross Sharkfin Col and use the same schrund rappel. The North Ridge then traverses a long way NORTH to the far end of the Boston Glacier and starts at a col with ground falling away on both sides. This route turns WEST after a short traverse and starts under a face. If you walked past a rock buttress and kept going, you have gone to the North Ridge.

A GENUINE NAMING TRAP, WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE CAMP: Forbidden's 'northeast face route' is sometimes used loosely to mean a HIGH TRAVERSE BELOW THE EAST RIDGE that skirts the gendarmes — an easier, quite different line, and the one some descent descriptions mean. This route is the technical ice-patch face above the Boston Glacier. If the description you are following has you traversing under a ridge crest rather than climbing a face, you are reading about the other thing.

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col, then the connecting ridge
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft at about mile 21.7 of Cascade River Road, the unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and slide alder into Boston Basin, roughly 3.2 miles and 3,100 ft. Most parties camp at high camp near 6,400 ft; the low camp near 5,300 ft works for slower groups. Sahale Glacier Camp on the other side of the ridge serves the same objective for parties coming over Cascade Pass.

An alpine start is standard. Rope up the QUIEN SABE GLACIER — the big crevasses are low on the glacier and the direct line through them runs to about 45 degrees and is very exposed, so most parties take the left side and traverse in beneath Sharkfin Tower. Later in the season, end-run the bergschrund below the col by traversing climber's right, then cut back up-left above it to gain the SAHALE-BOSTON COL at about 8,200 ft.

From the col the route follows the connecting ridge toward Boston: flat at first, then widening onto loose rock, staying generally right and on the crest.

The difficulty here is the rock quality, not the grade. This peak has a real fatality history and the descent — three rappels off fixed slings down the southeast side — should not be treated casually.
hazards: Crevasses on the Quien Sabe, with a potentially poorly bridged bergschrund below the col that worsens through the season
Notoriously loose and rotten rock, with rockfall onto and within the party
Essentially unprotectable class 4 with real exposure on the knife-edge section
A short but exposed snow traverse on the col that wants axe and crampons
Aging natural rappel anchors on the descent — slung horns and blocks, not bolts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SAHALE-BOSTON COL AT ABOUT 8,200 FT, AND THE COL IS THE ONE THING ON THIS ROUTE THAT IS HARD TO MISTAKE: it is the saddle shared with the Sahale trade route, so it carries traffic and it has ground falling away on both sides. If you gained a high point rather than a saddle, you are not there.

THE APPROACH TEST IS THE BERGSCHRUND. Later in the season the way onto the col is to traverse climber's RIGHT to end-run the schrund and then cut back up-LEFT above it. A party that walked onto the col without meeting a schrund has almost certainly come up in early-season conditions — fine, but it means the position cannot be confirmed that way and the ridge itself has to do it.

THE COUNTABLE SEQUENCE ON THE RIDGE, AND THE FALSE SUMMIT IS THE POINT OF IT: the crest steepens, widens, and then narrows to a KNIFE EDGE — that is where the route becomes genuinely exposed. At the high point of that ridge a FALSE SUMMIT stands in front of you. YOU DO NOT CLIMB IT. Make the class 4 downclimbing moves and follow the cairned line along the cliff edge to the RIGHT (east) around it. After about 100 ft of that bypass the Boston Glacier and the true summit pyramid come into view for the first time.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS THE LAST ONE, AND IT WORKS IN FOG: YOU CROSS ABOUT 200 FT OF GLACIER ABOVE A BERGSCHRUND IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE FINAL SUMMIT BLOCK. If you are scrambling loose rock to a high point and you have NOT crossed snow above a schrund in the last few minutes, that high point is the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

THE LAST FEATURE BEFORE THE TOP is a small ledge on the LEFT just short of the summit block, sometimes with a moat at it; above that it is class 3 on loose rock to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: The Quien Sabe's northwest corner to the lower of the two gullies
approach_variants.season: Condition-dependent rather than calendar-dependent — documented ascents span a September first ascent on steep snow and a February first winter ascent
approach_variants.notes:
In winter the recorded approach is Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead gate, then bike or ski up the Cascade Pass trail to the highest switchback near 6,400 ft, angling up and dropping into the Soldier Boy drainage, then a rising traverse to the QUIEN SABE GLACIER'S NORTHWEST CORNER. Rope up for the glacier crossing. In summer the standard Boston Basin approach reaches the same ground.

The face is used deliberately as the lower-consequence alternative to the Southeast Face when that side is too icy and too unprotected — which is worth knowing, because it means a party may arrive here having changed its mind rather than having planned it.

Five pitches: two of steep snow heading northeast, a large gully east on the third, a fourth to about 200 ft north of the summit, and a fifth across an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top.
hazards: A bergschrund near the base of the face
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe Glacier approach
Rime ice needing removal before anything can be climbed or protected, on the winter ascent
Rock bands between the gullies that are poor rock and poor protection — the gullies themselves protect better than the face between them
Loose rock characteristic of this peak, especially on the summit rock step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE GULLIES: THERE ARE TWO PROMINENT ONES ON THIS FACE AND THE ROUTE TAKES THE LOWER. That is the one countable fact published about the start and it is the one to carry. A party at the base of the other gully is on a different piece of the face, with the rock band between them as the divider.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS THE SCHRUND, AND ITS SOLUTION IS DIRECTIONAL: the bergschrund at the base is turned by climbing to CLIMBER'S RIGHT. If your way past the schrund went left, re-examine which gully you are under.

COUNT THE FIRST TWO BELAYS, WHICH ARE DESCRIBED BY WHAT THEY SIT UNDER RATHER THAN BY HEIGHT: two pitches of steep snow head NORTHEAST, the first belay UNDER A BULGE and the second WHERE A GULLY OPENS TO THE EAST. If your second stance is not at a place where a gully opens away east, the line is wrong.

AND YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN IF YOU CROSSED A COL. The Southeast Face — the standard route — is reached over the Sahale-Boston col at about 8,200 ft and shares that saddle with the Sahale trade route. This face is climbed straight off the northwest corner of the Quien Sabe with no col crossed at all. If you walked over a saddle to get where you are standing, you are under the standard route, not this one.

THE FINISH CONFIRMS IT: pitch four tops out about 200 ft NORTH of the summit and the last pitch crosses an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top. A route that deposits you on the summit directly has not been this one.

approach_variants.name: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, the same window as the Southeast Ridge; being steeper rock it sheds snow a little faster after an early-season storm
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small unsigned Boston Basin pulloff near 3,200-3,300 ft. The old mining road runs about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, then an unmaintained but well-travelled boot path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams — top off bottles there — to treeline around 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on the knoll above the green meadows at 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up and traverse EAST along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully below the tower. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left give an alternate entry and rejoin the couloir about 100 ft up.

There is no separate approach to the Southeast FACE. You reach it by climbing the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and rappelling.
hazards: Getting into the wrong gully: on 10 July 2005 a six-person party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here, a climber was struck by rockfall during the roped traverse back toward the standard line, and minutes later a natural boulder anchor failed during the retreat rappel, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth
Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier
The two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains and no rap rings, and there is no anchor at all at the very base of pitch 1
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food canisters required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS FACE IS NOT WALKED TO. IT IS RAPPELLED INTO — and that is the cleanest test on the whole tower. A party standing at its start has already climbed the first two pitches of the SOUTHEAST RIDGE and made two rappels of about 75 ft each from the fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2. A party that WALKED to where it is standing is at the Southeast Ridge notch, one route to the side.

YOU CAN SEE THE FACE FROM THAT NOTCH, WHICH IS WHY THE MIX-UP HAPPENS: the clean southeast face is visible from the base of the Southeast Ridge and looks approachable. It is not, from there.

IDENTIFY THE RIDGE NOTCH BY ITS ANCHOR, NOT BY ITS SHAPE: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 carries NO chains and NO rap rings. That absence is a positive identification, and it is also a planning fact — you will be leaving a biner, a ring or a short cord to get down.

BEFORE ANY OF THAT, GET THE APPROACH GULLY RIGHT, BECAUSE THIS IS WHERE PEOPLE HAVE DIED. Traverse east along the TOP of the Quien Sabe several hundred feet; the correct gully leads to a SNOW PATCH DIRECTLY AT THE TOWER'S BASE and then a short gully to the notch. A similar-looking gully nearby does not. If your gully does not deliver you to a snow patch at the foot of the tower, stop and re-check rather than continuing or traversing across — the 2005 accident happened during exactly that correction, not during the mistake.

CONFIRM ON THE FIRST MOVES OF THE FACE ITSELF: pitch 1 steps onto a DETACHED BLOCK and then follows a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just LEFT of the arete to a bolted anchor in a notch. If you are not standing on a detached block, you are not on this pitch.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; July and August are the most settled, and snow can linger around camp into July
approach_variants.notes:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a filing error.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
hazards: Rockfall off the ridge and the tower is the primary hazard
Weather that builds fast, with afternoon thunderstorms usual
A very small, exposed tower top that many parties choose not to stand on
Approach terrain shared with Forbidden's West Ridge descent, so parties may be above you in the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FORMATION IS THE EASY PART: THE AIGUILLE IS CONSPICUOUS ON ENTERING BOSTON BASIN and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

THE BASE IS THE NOTCH TO THE RIGHT OF THE NORTH RIDGE — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

COUNT THE PITCHES, BECAUSE THE COUNT IS THE ROUTE: THREE TO FOUR PITCHES OF FOURTH-CLASS SCRAMBLING TO THE BASE OF A TOWER, AND THEN ONE 40-FT PITCH TO ITS TOP. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE TOP IS THAT IT IS NOT THE TOP. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

TELL IT FROM THE SOUTH RIDGE BY WHICH SIDE YOU WALKED ROUND. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.
approach_variants.hours: Half a day from Boston Basin camp

approach_variants.name: Eldorado ice cap to Klawatti Col, then the buttress that stands directly above camp
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the Inspiration Glacier traverse and the moat at the foot of the buttress are reliably crossable
approach_variants.notes:
The whole approach is the Eldorado one: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep unmaintained boot path through old growth to the boulder field, and up into Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek basin. Camp there or push on to the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,500-7,600 ft.

From that camp the day is glacier travel, not a trail. Rope up, cross the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit, and continue north-northeast to KLAWATTI COL at about 7,800 ft, the saddle dividing the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on Klawatti Peak's south side. This traverse is the navigational crux of the whole route — it is flat, featureless and whiteouts are routine, so carry a bearing or a track and be prepared to navigate blind. Parties commonly camp at the col itself.

Three Klawatti routes leave from cols within half a mile of each other, and the baseFinding below is about telling them apart rather than about the walking. A wilderness permit for the Klawatti zone comes from the Marblemount ranger station.
hazards: Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers, worst near Eldorado's east ridge
Whiteout navigation on a flat, featureless ice cap with no handrail
A moat at the foot of the buttress where the glacier has pulled back from the rock
Rock repeatedly described as lousy and loose — test every hold rather than trusting the grade
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BUTTRESS STANDS DIRECTLY ABOVE THE KLAWATTI CAMP AND IS MINUTES FROM IT — not a traverse away. That is the first thing that separates it from the peak's other two routes. If you have walked more than a few minutes from the saddle you have started the wrong climb.

THE DECIDING TEST IS WHAT IS ABOVE THE MOAT, AND IT IS A ONE-LOOK TEST. Cross the moat and the ground above is ROCK and keeps being rock: two or three short low-fifth pitches, then class 4, then scrambling. IF THERE ARE SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET OF 40-55 DEGREE SNOW ABOVE A SHORT ROCK STEP, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTH-FACING SNOW LINE THIS CATALOG FILES AS THE SOUTHEAST FACE, which starts from the same col and is a snow climb with one rock move rather than a rock climb. That difference decides whether you needed a rack or a second tool.

THE THIRD ROUTE IS AT A DIFFERENT COL ENTIRELY. The North Ridge starts from the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, roughly 0.4 mile further along under Klawatti's west face — a separate notch a hundred feet higher, and one you have to solve rather than walk through. If you are walking a ridge crest north with a rock tower ahead of you, you have gone past this route to that one.

WHAT THE COL LOOKS LIKE: a broad saddle with usable bivy sites on the south side, and the LOW point between the Klawatti Glacier on one side and the McAllister on the other — so from it you can see down both. A spot where the ground only falls away one way is not the col.

approach_variants.name: Klawatti Col and the south flank to the bergschrund below the face
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Aug once the schrund bridges have consolidated; a separate Apr-Jun window exists for the face as a firm corn-snow line
approach_variants.notes:
Identical approach to the SW Buttress as far as the col: Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the Cascade River log crossing, the steep timbered climbers' path, the boulder field (stay climber's right — cairn lines trending left lead into cliffier ground), the basin at 5,500-5,800 ft, then Roush Creek and bivy sites at 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up there.

Climb the Eldorado Glacier, then make the long, mostly flat traverse east and north across the Inspiration Glacier to KLAWATTI COL at about 7,800 ft. Reckon roughly 7-8 miles and over 6,500 ft of gain one way from the car to the foot of the climb, normally split over two or three days.

From the col a short direct climb up the peak's south-facing flank reaches the base. Parties leave the col around 4 a.m. on purpose: this is a south-facing snow slope, icy in the pre-dawn shade and softening fast once the sun is on it, and it is roughly an hour and a half up and an hour down from the col.
hazards: A bergschrund, and later in the season a moat, guarding the base of the face
Several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow directly above the schrund, on ground where a slip does not stop
South aspect: icy before dawn, softening and wet-sliding by mid-morning
Whiteout on the Inspiration Glacier both ways — parties have been caught out right at the summit
A crumbly, elongated summit where the true high point is genuinely hard to identify
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BERGSCHRUND, AND THE SCHRUND IS THE ROUTE'S IDENTITY. From Klawatti Col you climb directly up the south flank until the snow pulls back from the rock. That gap — a schrund early, a moat late — is where the climbing starts, and the short 4th-to-easy-5th rock step that clears it is the technical crux of the whole route.

YOU MUST BE AT THE COL ITSELF: if you are not standing at the LOW POINT of the ridge dividing the Inspiration and McAllister glacier systems, you are not below this route.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHAT COMES AFTER THE STEP: SNOW, AND A LOT OF IT. Above the rock step the route is several hundred feet of 40 to 55 degree snow — through a constriction, steepening over a pseudo-cornice bulge on the upper southwest side — to the top of the face, then an easy walk along the southwest ridge. IF THE ROCK KEEPS GOING ABOVE THE STEP, a second and third pitch of it and no snow slope, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTHWEST BUTTRESS, which leaves from the same col. One of these wants a rack, the other wants a picket and possibly a second tool.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION THAT ALSO SERVES THE DESCENT: parties have found rappel slings on the EAST side of the constriction at the moat. A moat with old tat on its east side is the right one.

DO NOT WALK ON PAST THE COL. The North Ridge leaves from the Klawatti-Austera col about 0.4 mile further, and the ground there is a ridge crest, not a snow face. If you can see a rock tower standing up on the crest ahead of you, you have overshot by a col.

AT THE TOP THE SUMMIT IS THE HARD PART TO IDENTIFY, NOT THE BASE: the crest is crumbly and elongated, at least one party found no register and could not settle which bump was highest, and cairns mark a line back down the ridge toward the col. Note that line on the way up — it is the alternative to reversing the face.

approach_variants.name: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, when the crest and the connecting cols are snow-free enough to scramble
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,150 ft, then the standard Eldorado climbers' path: forest, boulder field, treeline, and camps in Eldorado Basin / Roush Creek around 6,000-6,300 ft. Climb the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge near 7,500 ft, then traverse roughly a mile and a half north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft.

Klawatti Col is NOT the start of this route. Continue past it, along a lobe of the McAllister Glacier under Klawatti Peak's WEST FACE, about 0.4 mile to the next break in the ridge — the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA COL at about 7,900 ft. The scramble takes about an hour from that col, up to two hours if you count from Klawatti Col.
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration and the upper McAllister lobe
A moat at the Klawatti-Austera col that ranges from class 4 to class 5 depending on where you cross it
Exposure on narrow sections of the crest, where route-finding is what keeps the grade at third class
Loose rock on the ledge traverses around The Smokestack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE COLS: YOU WANT THE SECOND ONE. Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft is where the peak's other two routes start; this route starts at the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, a further 0.4 mile north along the foot of Klawatti's west face and a hundred feet higher.

THE SECOND COL IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY BEING A PROBLEM, AND IT OFFERS A CHOICE OF TWO CROSSINGS — WHICH IS ITSELF THE CONFIRMATION. Receding snow leaves a moat here. The LOWEST notch is class 5 downclimbing; a crossing to the RIGHT (southeast) of the lowest notch is class 4. Parties have also found an old rappel anchor at this col and used it. A col you walked over without choosing between two ways down is Klawatti Col, one short.

GAIN THE LOWER RIDGE ON ITS EAST SIDE — the crest itself is harder than it needs to be low down, and the east flank is the easy way onto it.

THE SMOKESTACK IS THE CONFIRMING LANDMARK AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE. Class 3 scrambling up the crest brings you to a rock tower around 8,400 ft that the route is named around. YOU DO NOT CLIMB IT: go round it on its WEST side by a short gully and regain the crest above. A party that has climbed a tower on the ridge rather than walked around it has gone off route. A party that reached the summit without ever passing a tower was never on the North Ridge.

NEGATIVE TEST FOR THE OTHER DIRECTION: if the ground in front of you is a snow face rather than a ridge crest, you are below the south-facing snow line and one col too far south.

WHAT IS THIN HERE, SAID PLAINLY: this ridge is barely written up. The col elevations, the Smokestack and the east-side start come from the route's own record; the detail about the two crossings at the moat and the old anchor comes from accounts that could not be retrieved in full, so treat the crossing description as a warning to expect a choice rather than as a promise about which side is easier this year.

approach_variants.name: Three glaciers and two cols to the Klawatti-Austera notch, then the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul to Aug, while the notch is still bridged and the three glacier crossings are consolidated
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near mile 20 (about 2,100 ft) and find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence — it has been rebuilt repeatedly after flood damage and can be an awkward single log, so scout it before committing. On the far bank the unsigned climbers' path pushes through swampy brush and devil's club into open old growth, gains roughly 1,500 ft, then breaks onto two wide talus fields. Above them an alpine meadow leads to a slabby ramp onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and put crampons on there.

Camp at Eldorado Creek Basin around 5,600 ft, Roush Creek Basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, or push to a high camp near Eldorado's East Ridge at 7,200-7,600 ft.

From high camp the day is three miles of sustained glacier travel across three basins and two cols: the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier (crevasses worst near Eldorado's east ridge), the upper Inspiration at about 7,800 ft to KLAWATTI COL, then past Klawatti Peak on its left and along the upper McAllister Glacier beneath Klawatti's west face for about 0.4 mile to the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA notch at about 7,900 ft. Guide figures for that leg are roughly 1,280 ft of ascent and 592 ft of descent over 2.8 miles, about four hours one way.

Austera Peak is the HIGH POINT OF THE AUSTERA TOWERS ARÊTE rather than a separate peak, which is why the top of this climb needs as much care as the bottom.
hazards: Crevasse fall on all three glaciers, worse as the season progresses and bridges soften
A moat gap at the Klawatti-Austera notch that often needs stemming or a rappel of about 75 ft to reach the upper Klawatti Glacier
Route-finding in flat light or whiteout on an open ice cap with no handrail
Loose rock on every exposed rock section of the tower — the false-summit approach is explicitly loose class 3
Rime and verglas icing the final chimney even in summer
A genuinely committing and remote position with long retreat times
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE KLAWATTI-AUSTERA NOTCH AT ABOUT 7,900 FT, AND YOU IDENTIFY IT BY COUNTING COLS, NOT BY LOOKING AT AUSTERA. From the Inspiration Glacier you cross Klawatti Col first at about 7,800 ft — that one is not it. Keep Klawatti Peak on your right, follow its west face along the McAllister Glacier for about 0.4 mile, and the SECOND break in the ridge is the one. It sits a hundred feet higher than the first.

THE NOTCH ANNOUNCES ITSELF BY BEING A PROBLEM. It is not a walk-through: a moat gap has to be stemmed or rappelled — about 75 ft — to get down onto the upper Klawatti Glacier. IF YOU STEPPED THROUGH A COL WITHOUT HAVING TO SOLVE ANYTHING, YOU ARE STILL AT KLAWATTI COL. Old anchors have been found at the right notch; treat them as aging tat and back them up rather than as proof of position.

ABOVE THE NOTCH, COUNT THREE THINGS IN ORDER: broken 4th-class rock off the notch, then a short cliff band that many parties bypass on scree and ledges to the RIGHT (east) rather than climbing direct, then the chockstone gully at the base of the summit tower.

THE HARDEST THING TO GET RIGHT ON THIS PEAK IS NOT THE BASE, IT IS THE TOP, AND THE CHIMNEY IS THE TEST. Parties routinely finish on a FALSE SUMMIT a few feet short of the true one. The true summit is reached only by crossing a narrow, exposed ridge between the two blocks and then climbing the CHOCKSTONE CHIMNEY — roughly THREE jammed chockstones in about 60 ft, stemming and face moves on the chimney's LEFT wall. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A NARROW RIDGE AND CLIMBED A CHIMNEY, THE POINT YOU ARE STANDING ON IS THE FALSE SUMMIT. A class 3+ ledge bypass on the peak's east side reaches the same notch without the chimney, so a party that took it has not gone wrong — but it has not confirmed its position either.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
approach_variants.season: Aug is the usual window; the timing is set by the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers being safely negotiable rather than by the rock
approach_variants.notes:
This is the same day out as the Southwest Ridge row on this peak and the two describe substantially the same ground — see _DEFECTS.

From the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,600 ft, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col. Tepeh Towers are passed along this same traverse. From the col, follow the ridge line along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where the standard sequence is a rappel of about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier, then a traverse high and left across it toward Austera.

This is meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado, and it is worth saying plainly: this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak, despite the catalog filing several of these objectives out of the same area.

Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête, not a free-standing summit, and it is the most accessible top in that group — which is exactly why parties end up on the wrong one.
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glacier traverses
A moat at the rappel point that has to work in both directions
Loose rock on the final summit tower
Rime or verglas on the final chimney even in summer
Exposed climbing on the closing pitches above a remote glacier, with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A BREAK IN THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,900 FT THAT YOU RAPPEL INTO, NOT WALK THROUGH. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

GET THERE BY COUNTING, NOT BY SIGHTING AUSTERA. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your LEFT through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the SECOND break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

ABOVE THE GLACIER TRAVERSE THE CLIMBING IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a SUB-SUMMIT, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the RIGHT on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS THE REAL HAZARD ON THIS PEAK, AND IT IS THE TEST THAT MATTERS. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. THE TRUE SUMMIT IS REACHED ONLY AFTER CROSSING A NARROW, OFTEN SNOWY RIDGE BETWEEN TWO BLOCKS AND CLIMBING A SHORT CHIMNEY OR A FEW FEET OF LOW FIFTH BEYOND IT. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

THE MOAT BESIDE THE RAPPEL POINT is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, while enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses; by late September the glacier is largely bare and the pass can be bullet ice and loose rock
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp around mile eight.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the bridge near McAllister Camp has been out in past years — check current NPS conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Leave the maintained trail at Tricouni Camp and climb the climbers' path up LUCKY RIDGE, the ridge between McAllister and Thunder creeks: roughly 4,000 ft of gain over a couple of miles through brush and devil's club, with two short cliff-band scrambles. Camp near the northeast corner of the proglacial lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier around 6,000 ft, with the icefall in view above.

Rope up around 7,000 ft on the flat snow shelf and climb the glacier's EASTERN margin — the central icefall splits the lower and upper tiers and has caught parties who drifted climber's-left.
hazards: A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises
The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin
Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season
Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely
A long, remote approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS LUCKY PASS AT ABOUT 7,200 FT, AND THE PASS IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY WHAT IT DIVIDES: it is the notch at the HEAD of the Borealis Glacier between Primus and Tricouni Peak, and the route to Tricouni splits off east from the same spot. If the ground only falls away on one side of you, you are not at the pass.

FROM THE PASS THE EAST SLOPE RISES DIRECTLY WEST — a bouldery class 3 slope, not a ridge crest and not a face. Trip reports describe the climbing above the pass as nothing more than a walk, which is the honest summary: the difficulty of this route is the creek, the brushy ridge and the glacier, all of which are behind you by the time you are at the pass.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ABOVE THE PASS THAT CAN GO WRONG. A false summit stands at about 8,270 ft. YOU TRAVERSE CLIMBER'S-LEFT AROUND IT — you do not go over it — and the true summit at 8,508 ft is beyond. If you reached a high point without having traversed around anything, you are 240 ft short.

NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTES, AND IT WORKS BEFORE YOU EVER LEAVE THE CAR: this route is the only one reached from the THUNDER CREEK side. The South Ridge is reached from the Eldorado ice cap across five glaciers, and the North Ridge from an unnamed glacier north of the peak. If you walked up a creek trail from a campground on Highway 20, you are on this one.

approach_variants.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
approach_variants.notes:
This is the long way to Primus and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the East Slope. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the North Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse east and north across it — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.
hazards: A heavily crevassed North Klawatti and McAllister glacier system, especially late season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August and September — probe before committing weight
Complex glacier route-finding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility
A short technical step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch that has to be reversed at the end of the day
Extreme remoteness: a multi-day approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ONE FINDABLE FEATURE ON THIS ROUTE IS THE NOTCH AT THE McALLISTER-KLAWATTI COL, AND IT IS FINDABLE BECAUSE IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ALL DAY YOU NEED A ROPE FOR ROCK. It is a step of roughly 50 ft: downclimbed, hand-lined, or rappelled off a sling on a horn or block — there is no fixed hardware. If you have crossed a col without a technical step, you are not through it yet.

AFTER THE NOTCH, THE TEST IS WHAT YOU ARE STANDING ON RATHER THAN WHAT YOU CAN SEE. You drop onto the NORTH KLAWATTI GLACIER and traverse east and north across it. The climbing begins where you take the rope OFF: snow-covered talus, class 2-3, straight to the 8,508 ft summit. There is no notch, no rib and no marked start above the glacier — the honest answer is that this route has no rock landmark at its base, and the col behind you is what tells you where you are.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONG ONE AND IT SETTLES THE WHOLE PEAK: THE OTHER STANDARD LINE ON PRIMUS IS REACHED FROM THUNDER CREEK, AND IT STARTS AT LUCKY PASS — a notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier where the route to Tricouni Peak splits off east. IF YOU ARE AT A PASS WITH A SECOND PEAK'S ROUTE LEAVING IT, YOU ARE ON THE EAST SLOPE AND YOU CAME UP THE WRONG VALLEY FOR THIS ROW. The two lines are on opposite sides of the mountain and share no ground below the summit.

AND WATCH THE FALSE SUMMIT WHATEVER SIDE YOU CAME FROM: a false top stands around 8,270 ft and is passed on climber's-left. A high point reached without traversing round anything is not the summit.

approach_variants.name: Round to the unnamed glacier north of the peak
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August; a documented late-September attempt found the crux notch glazed with bullet ice and the loose rock unbonded, which made the route markedly harder and more dangerous
approach_variants.notes:
This is a genuinely obscure line and every recorded approach to it is a variation on getting round to the mountain's NORTH side, which no other Primus route visits.

The first recorded ascent reached it from the Klawatti side: descend a couloir where the NORTH KLAWATTI GLACIER meets Primus's WEST RIDGE, then traverse an unnamed glacier north of Primus to the foot of the crest. The first-ascent account says in as many words that it was unlikely this approach had been used before.

Other parties have come from the Thunder Creek side instead — the same trailhead, ford and Lucky Ridge climb as the East Slope, to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the toe of the Borealis Glacier — and then reached the ridge by circling the glacial lake at the glacier's terminus and crossing a short section of glacier to the base, rather than climbing the glacier toward Lucky Pass. One party took that line specifically because conditions at the standard Primus-Tricouni saddle were hazardous that day.

The ridge itself is about 1,000 ft and took the first-ascent party roughly an hour.
hazards: Very loose, serrated rock along the entire crest — blocks and towers described as good but somewhat loose
A 5.6 crux notch with no fixed protection: natural gear and slung blocks only
Verglas glazing the notch in cool or wet weather, which is what defeated a late-September attempt
Committing retreat once above the crux — the recommended descent is the East Ridge to Lucky Pass, not this ridge
Glacier travel on an unnamed, rarely visited glacier with no established line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON, AND IT IS DECIDED BY WHETHER YOU HAD TO GO DOWN TO GET THERE. Every approach to this ridge involves LOSING height onto a glacier NORTH of Primus — down a couloir from the North Klawatti Glacier where it meets Primus's west ridge, or down and around the glacial lake at the Borealis Glacier's terminus. If your day has been a continuous climb, you have not reached this route.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE ONE TO CARRY: LUCKY PASS IS NOT THIS ROUTE. If you are standing at a col at about 7,200 ft at the head of the Borealis Glacier, with Tricouni Peak's route splitting off east, you are at the start of the East Slope — a class 3 walk. The North Ridge is reached by turning away from that pass, not through it.

WHAT THE BASE ITSELF LOOKS LIKE: the foot of a 1,000 ft crest of blocks and towers, met from a glacier rather than from a notch. There is no published cairn, marker or fixed anchor at the start; the ridge is very rarely repeated and nothing on it should be assumed to be in place.

CONFIRM ON THE GROUND YOU CLIMB, NOT ON THE APPROACH: the lower ridge is 3rd and 4th class blocks and towers; the upper ridge is BANDED ROCK at low fifth, and that banding is what the first-ascent party singled out. A ridge that stays third class to the summit is not this one — and a ridge that never carried you above a glacier on the peak's north side never was.

approach_variants.name: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
approach_variants.season: Once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower has opened enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late in the season — usually July or August, most often as part of an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Everything below the ice cap is the standard Eldorado approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, backtrack a short way along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River (a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts year to year), then the steep unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,000-3,500 ft through old growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine meadows of Eldorado Creek basin — commonly five to six hours from the car. Push on to the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,600 ft.

From that camp it is roughly a 45-minute roped glacier walk north-northwest to where the towers rise out of the icecap. The towers sit at the saddle you cross anyway to get from the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister — so most parties pass beneath them on the way to Klawatti, Austera or Dorado Needle and climb one as a side objective. Round trip from camp is well under two hours.

Be clear about what this row is: TEPEH TOWERS IS NOT ON ELDORADO PEAK, despite being filed under the same area. It is a separate formation further along the icecap.
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach — roped travel and crevasse rescue gear, not an unroped stroll
The moat where the glacier rests against the rock, which is the whole gate on this climb
Loose rock near the summit
Softening snow bridges on the return, which is the real time constraint on such a short objective
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TEPEH TOWERS IS AN ARÊTE OF MANY SPIRES, NOT ONE TOWER — that is the first thing to understand, and it is why the base finding here has to be about the moat rather than about the skyline. The formation is a rock arête poking out of the icecap northwest of the Inspiration Glacier, with Eldorado to the west and Klawatti to the northeast, and it carries a great many small spires.

SO THE PROCEDURE IS: CLIMB HIGH ON THE GLACIER UNTIL THE ICE IS RESTING AGAINST THE ROCK, AND CROSS THE MOAT THERE. You are looking for the point where the snow meets the rock cleanly enough to step across; that point, not a particular spire seen from a distance, is what you navigate to.

THE POSITIVE CONFIRMATION IS FIXED GEAR, AND IT IS THE ONLY DISCRIMINATOR PUBLISHED FOR THIS FORMATION: THE TOWER PARTIES CLIMB HAS RAPPEL ANCHORS DIRECTLY BELOW ITS SUMMIT. If you top out and there is no anchor below you, you have climbed a neighbouring spire — which is not dangerous here, but it is not the recorded line either.

THE LENGTH TEST IS SHORT AND UNAMBIGUOUS: ONE short low-fifth pitch above the moat, then scrambling to the top. If you are running out a second and third rope length, you are on something else on the same arête.

WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT KNOWN: no published source names which of the spires is the climbed one or gives a way to tell it from its neighbours at a distance. That gap is stated here rather than filled — treat the anchor below the summit as the confirmation and the moat as the navigation.

approach_variants.name: Over the ice cap to Dorado Needle Col, then down into Marble Creek Cirque
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer once fully snow-free, with maximum daylight for a long climbing day; Cascade River Road is often not open until late June
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, and gain the Eldorado Glacier. Most parties treat this as three days: approach, climb, exit, with a base camp at the East Ridge site near 7,500 ft or on the western margin of the Eldorado Glacier.

The defining feature of the approach is that you must get DOWN to the base. The line runs from the ice cap across to the Dorado Needle Col area, then a loose fourth-class downclimb — accounts on the neighbouring line describe rappelling, steep névé downclimbing and moat work over roughly 1,000 ft of descent — into the MARBLE CREEK CIRQUE on Eldorado's west side, and the toe of the ridge is at the bottom of that.

This is a long day: parties have taken up to about 17 hours round trip from the East Ridge base camp, and an unplanned bivouac is a real possibility if the middle section goes slowly.

A warning from parties who have done it: published route descriptions for this arête have been called inaccurate and sandbagged, and at least one party went off route immediately as a result. Trust the terrain over the topo.
hazards: A loose fourth-class downclimb into the cirque that has to be reversed or bypassed at the end of the day
Rockfall and loose rock over the full length of the arête, including the opening pitch
Large moats on both sides of the ridge at its foot, and a building-sized snow remnant to keep clear of
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers that open through the summer
A confusing middle section where slow progress turns into a bivouac
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE BY GOING DOWN, NOT UP, AND THAT IS THE FIRST CHECK. The toe of the arête sits at roughly 6,000 ft in the Marble Creek Cirque, reached only by a loose fourth-class downclimb off the Dorado Needle Col area. If your approach has been a continuous ascent from camp, you have not reached this route.

THE SEQUENCE AT THE BOTTOM IS COUNTABLE AND IT IS THE POSITIVE TEST: from the snow at the base, spooky scrambling on GLACIER-POLISHED SLABS leads to a STEEP, OPEN CHIMNEY FEATURE. Slabs first, chimney second. The rock climbing proper begins a couple of hundred feet above the toe of the ridge on its NORTH side.

THE FIRST PITCH CONFIRMS IT BY BEING BAD. The opening pitch is unbelievably loose 5.6 on the ridge crest. If your first pitch is clean and solid, you are on the wrong feature.

THERE IS A HARDER LINE ON THE SAME WALL AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: the SOUTHWEST ARÊTE — climbed in full only in 2022, about 3,600 ft at grade V 5.10 — takes the same cirque approach and a different arête. This route is the shorter 1969 line at about 2,800 ft, sustained 5.6-5.7 with an old-school 5.8 crux. IF THE CLIMBING IS RELENTLESSLY HARDER THAN MID-FIFTH FROM LOW DOWN, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG ARÊTE.

CONFIRM AT THE CRUX: a set of rocky towers ends in a face traverse protected by a SINGLE IN-SITU PITON. One piton, one traverse. That is the hardest move on the route and it is the landmark for the upper half.

approach_variants.name: Down the Inspiration Glacier to the ice-couloir notch, then snow onto the crest
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ridge is largely snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Eldorado one to the high camp on the Inspiration Glacier: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep boot path, the boulder field, Eldorado Creek basin, and up the Eldorado Glacier to the East Ridge camp near 7,500-7,600 ft.

From camp, the route goes DOWN before it goes up. Descend the Inspiration Glacier toward the notch used as the rappel point for the Northwest Ice Couloir — an obvious gap between the North Ridge and the first rock spire, at about 8,100 ft — and climb steep snow from there onto the North Ridge proper.

The ridge follows generally solid rock on its EASTERN aspect with good friction and incut holds, so the exposure toward the glacier side stays modest while the drop to the west is dramatic. Near the top you can finish directly up steeper ice and rock or join the classic East Ridge finish.
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier both on the way to the notch and on the way back
Loose rock in places along the crest
Wind exposure high on the ridge
Wet rock, which raises the difficulty of this route noticeably rather than marginally
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS THE LANDMARK, AND IT IS SHARED WITH ANOTHER ROUTE — WHICH IS WHY THE TEST IS WHAT YOU DO THERE, NOT WHERE YOU STAND. The gap you are looking for is the obvious notch between the North Ridge and the FIRST ROCK SPIRE along the crest, at about 8,100 ft, reached by descending the Inspiration Glacier from the East Ridge camp. That same notch is the rappel station for the Northwest Ice Couloir.

SO: AT THE NOTCH, IF YOU ARE PUTTING A ROPE THROUGH AN ANCHOR AND GOING DOWN INTO THE CIRQUE ON THE OTHER SIDE, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHWEST COULOIR. IF YOU ARE CLIMBING STEEP SNOW UP OUT OF THE NOTCH ONTO A ROCK CREST, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH RIDGE. Two routes, one notch, opposite directions.

THE ROCK TELLS YOU WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST TO BE ON, AND THAT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER. This route stays on the ridge's EAST side — clean, solid rock with good friction and incut holds, snow on the northeast face below you keeping the exposure feeling manageable. IF THE DROP IS ON BOTH SIDES OR YOU HAVE DRIFTED WEST INTO SERIOUS AIR AND WORSE ROCK, COME BACK EAST.

WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT PUBLISHED: no source names a single fixed starting point on this crest — one description says simply to climb the path of least resistance from your point of choice on the ridge. The notch is the findable thing; above it, the route is defined by staying east on the good rock rather than by a marked start. Sources also disagree on the grade, 5.6 against 5.7, so do not read a hard move as evidence you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Rappel off the ice cap into the Marble Creek cirque, then the couloir splitting the northwest face
approach_variants.season: Highly conditions-dependent. Early season, roughly May-June, can give steep thin ice and moderate mixed; mid-to-late summer the couloir is usually mostly snow with a few ice steps; a good cold snap in late October or November can bring in firm, well-bonded ice. Grade moves with it, roughly AI2-3 up to WI3 in lean conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

From there this route diverges: rather than continuing over the ridge into Roush Basin for the standard camp, traverse the Roush Divide and ascend the Eldorado Glacier, trending toward the mountain's northwest side and the wild Marble Creek Cirque. High camp is either in Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek Basin or at the Eldorado-Inspiration site near 7,500-7,600 ft.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch some accounts call the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and RAPPEL from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One recorded single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.
hazards: An extreme funnel: the whole face feeds into a narrow confined couloir, so anything the leader dislodges lands on the belay
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers and a long featureless crossing that is disorienting in whiteout
A moat or bergschrund where the glacier meets the couloir, widening through the summer
Cornices and crevasses at the couloir's exit near the knife-edge ridge
Rappelling the couloir is the only retreat once you are high, and it is slow — the practical escape is over the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ONCE YOU ARE IN THE CIRQUE THE ROUTE IS OBVIOUS, AND TWO SEPARATE PARTIES SAY SO IN NEARLY THE SAME WORDS: on looking up from below the rappel, one recorded instantly seeing the line — steep, fat and unmistakable. THE COULOIR SPLITS THE NORTHWEST FACE and there is nothing else in the cirque it could be confused with. So the navigation problem is not identifying the couloir; it is getting into the cirque at all.

THE NOTCH IS THE THING TO FIND, AND IT IS SHARED WITH THE NORTH RIDGE. It is the obvious gap between the North Ridge and the FIRST ROCK SPIRE, at about 8,100 ft, reached by traversing north from the East Ridge glacier track. AT THAT NOTCH THE TWO ROUTES GO OPPOSITE WAYS: rappel down the far side into the cirque and you are on this route; climb steep snow up onto the rock crest and you are on the North Ridge.

THE BASE ITSELF IS THE TRANSITION AT ABOUT 7,800 FT where the couloir meets the glacier — which is the usual place to find the moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier BEFORE you reach it.

ONE BRANCH POINT WORTH KNOWING: at least one party climbed a steep line just to CLIMBER'S LEFT of the main gut of the couloir rather than the gut itself. Both go; the gut is the route as described.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMBING: the line runs from about 7,800 ft to about 8,800 ft, roughly 1,000 ft, commonly described as eight 60 m pitches, and the character is a succession of short ice steps broken by lower-angle snow rather than one continuous wall. Steps around 70-80 degrees with occasional near-vertical bulges for a body length is right; sustained vertical ice for a full pitch is not this route in any season.

approach_variants.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the TEPEH TOWERS saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SMALL COL AT THE TOE OF THE RIDGE, AT THE TOP OF THE McALLISTER GLACIER'S 30-DEGREE APRON, AND THE THING DIRECTLY ABOVE IT IS A LINE OF GENDARMES ON THE CREST. Gendarmes on the skyline above a small col at the top of the apron is the confirmation.

CROSS THE MOAT AT THE COL, NOT AT THE SNOW GULLY. There is an alternative snow gully nearby that parties sometimes use to gain the ridge, and it is guarded by a LARGE MOAT that usually still needs a short rappel to bypass. The route's own start is easy fifth-class rock straight off the small col at the toe. If you are eyeing a snow gully with a big gap at its head, you are looking at the alternative, not the route.

THE LENGTH TEST IS DECISIVE ON THIS PEAK BECAUSE THE FOUR ROUTES ARE WILDLY DIFFERENT LENGTHS: this one is THREE pitches, each WELL UNDER 25 m. If you are running full rope lengths, or if you are still climbing after three, you are on the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from the other side) or the East Ridge (a long day off a different col).

A FIXED-GEAR CONFIRMATION, AND A WARNING WITH IT: the crest carries a lot of OLD FIXED SLINGS ON ROCK HORNS left by earlier parties, and higher up a PITON marks a slabby section leading to a V-SLOT GULLY. Plenty of tat on horns is a sign you are on the trade line — but it is aging tat, an anchor block has failed here before, and it should be backed up rather than trusted.

AND KNOW WHICH SIDE OF THE NEEDLE YOU ARE ON: this route is reached by climbing the McAllister's apron NORTHWEST. The Southwest Buttress lines are reached by continuing to the MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS and dropping about 700 vertical ft to a snow gully below it. The East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle. Three different cols; check which one you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
approach_variants.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
approach_variants.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 VERTICAL FEET BELOW THAT PASS and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS AT THE FOOT OF A PROMINENT, OFTEN YEAR-ROUND SNOW GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS LOCATED BY DESCENDING — IT STARTS ABOUT 700 VERTICAL FEET BELOW THE MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

AT THE TOP OF THAT GULLY THERE IS A FORK, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ON THIS PEAK MOST WORTH GETTING RIGHT. THIS ROUTE GOES AROUND TO THE RIGHT. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes STRAIGHT UP from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS PUBLISHED AS A WARNING AND IT IS WORTH CARRYING VERBATIM: DO NOT CLIMB DIRECTLY BELOW THE RIDGE CREST AT THE START.
