That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 OVERHANGING TERRAIN ON LOOSE ROCK. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

CONFIRM ON PITCH ONE: it is a FULL rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly RIGHT, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

AND CONFIRM BY WHICH COL YOU CROSSED: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

approach_variants.name: Same gully as the standard buttress — the difference is one turn at its top
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, when the approach glaciers are consolidated and the buttress is snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Southwest Buttress's, without exception: from the Cascade River Road trailhead near 2,100 ft, cross the river, climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado / Roush Creek Basin, and on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — about 5.8 miles and 5,500 ft from the car.

From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (the best passage is on its skier's right side near the steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent, often snow-filled gully that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress. A rope may be wanted here: a moat guarding the base can present an exposed, deep gap.

Everything to this point is shared with the 1985 standard line. The two routes part company at the top of the gully, and after two pitches they rejoin.
hazards: Crevasse and moat crossings on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
A long, remote approach with no easy bail once you are on the buttress
Sustained 5.10 low on the route, which is the wrong place to discover the crux pitch is wet
Loose rock on the upper pitches once the two routes have rejoined
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TWO ROUTES SHARE EVERY STEP OF THE APPROACH AND SEPARATE AT ONE POINT: THE TOP OF THE SNOW GULLY. THE STANDARD SOUTHWEST BUTTRESS TRAVERSES AROUND TO THE RIGHT THERE. THIS ROUTE GOES STRAIGHT UP.

AND THEN THE CONFIRMATION IS COUNTABLE, WHICH IS AS GOOD AS THIS GETS ON AN ALPINE ROUTE: two direct-start pitches of fourth and low-fifth scrambling lead to THREE VERTICAL CRACKS. YOU CLIMB THE RIGHTMOST OF THE THREE. Not the left, not the middle — the rightmost, which starts around 5.8, turns strenuous at 5.10, and finishes with a MANTEL ONTO A LARGE BENCH.

SO THE TEST IS: COUNT TO THREE, TAKE THE RIGHT-HAND ONE, AND EXPECT A MANTEL. If there are not three cracks in front of you, you have gone right at the top of the gully and you are on the standard line — a fine route, two grades easier, and the one you will end up on anyway.

THE SECOND PITCH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER: awkward 5.8+ climbing rejoins the original 1985 route AT A LARGE WHITE SLABBY ROCK. That white slab is the merge point and it is named in the route's own description. Once you are past it, the two lines are one and the remaining pitches to the summit ridge are the standard route's.

SO THE DIRECT START IS TWO PITCHES LONG. IF YOU ARE THREE OR FOUR PITCHES IN AND STILL LOOKING FOR THE MERGE, YOU HAVE MISSED THE WHITE SLAB — the merge is early, not high.

approach_variants.name: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
approach_variants.season: July through September, once glacier bridges and moats have stabilised but before the early-season storms return
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,100 ft — the first ten miles paved, the rest rough gravel and high-clearance recommended. Hike the Eldorado climbers' trail through forest, cross the creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft, roughly four miles and 6,000 ft of gain.

From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the COL BETWEEN POINT 8386 AND DORADO NEEDLE at about 7,600 ft. That col is the base.

Most parties take eight to twelve hours round trip from high camp, and descend by the Northwest Ridge rather than reversing this line — which means the day ends on unfamiliar ground with rappels and a moat, so scout the Northwest Ridge's top as you pass it.
hazards: Crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
Loose, thinly protectable rock on the first pitch off the col — test every placement
A bottomless moat on the glacier traverse partway up the route, where the line steps off the ridge and back on
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NAMED COL: THE ONE BETWEEN POINT 8386 AND DORADO NEEDLE, AT ABOUT 7,600 FT. The climbing starts immediately off it — steep, exposed mid-fifth moves straight from the col, no walk-in. IF YOU HAD TO TRAVEL FURTHER ALONG THE GLACIER AFTER CROSSING A COL BEFORE YOU FOUND ROCK, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG COL.

THE FIRST PITCH IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY BEING NASTY AND BY CARRYING A MARKER: it is a loose, poorly protectable 5.5, and A HORN WITH AN EXISTING SLING SITS ABOUT 100 FT UP. Loose rock plus a slung horn a rope-length up is the confirmation.

THERE IS AN ALTERNATIVE START AND IT HAS ITS OWN LANDMARK: a line beneath the 'CANNONBALL HOLE' to the RIGHT avoids that first loose section, at the cost of a moat crossing. A hole in the rock you could name is not a feature you find by accident — if you can see it, you are in the right place and you have a choice to make.

TELL IT FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS BY LENGTH AND BY DIFFICULTY, BECAUSE ALL FOUR ROUTES ON THIS NEEDLE ARE DIFFERENT SIZES. This one is longer and a bit harder than the Northwest Ridge (three short pitches from a small col at the top of the McAllister apron) and easier than the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from a gully 700 ft below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass). It follows the CENTRE portion of the rock on an obvious ridge line.

THE ROUTE STEPS OFF THE RIDGE PARTWAY UP AND THAT IS EXPECTED, NOT AN ERROR: after several ropelengths of class 3-4 you descend into a notch, traverse the glacier, and regain the ridge at a LEDGE MARKED BY QUARTZITE BANDS. Watch for a bottomless moat there. Pale banded rock on a ledge is the marker to aim for.

AND THE FINISH IS COUNTABLE: two short rappels drop into the notch below the true summit, then TWO sustained 5.7 crack pitches to the top. If you have climbed one hard pitch and stood on a summit, you were on the sub-summit tower.

approach_variants.name: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, once the road is open and the lower couloir approach holds consolidated snow
approach_variants.notes:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb PARTWAY up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the RIGHT, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.
hazards: Hanging glaciers above the route — the Sill Glacier among them — that release ice and rock; parties describe rocks and ice bouncing for three or four seconds at a time
The mountain's standing reputation for rockfall, with loose rock reported across trip reports and a documented near-miss on a 2020 descent
Steep 45-60 degree snow on approach and descent with real fall consequence — one report calls the heather descent the most dangerous part of the trip
A Cascade River ford at the very start, which rises through the day
A routefinding-intensive descent with suspect rappel anchors, and a history of parties returning a day or two late
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST FOR THIS ROUTE IS WHETHER YOU ARE TOUCHING VEGETATION, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST DISCRIMINATOR ON THE WHOLE FACE. This side of Johannesburg carries at least five named lines within a few hundred metres of each other, and most of them start with hundreds of feet of vertical bushwhacking — alder, turf, tree roots, tunnelling through near-vertical pines. THIS ROUTE DOES NOT. Its own published description ends with the words no bush climbing. IF YOU ARE PULLING ON TREES OR HEATHER TO MAKE UPWARD PROGRESS, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHEAST RIB OR THE NORTHEAST BUTTRESS, NOT ON THIS.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: STAY IN THE COULOIR. Do not break out onto rock low down. Climb the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir until a HANGING GLACIER appears on your RIGHT — that glacier is the landmark, and it is what you leave the couloir for. The Northeast Rib lines leave the couloir far lower, before it narrows.

FROM THE HANGING GLACIER, TAKE THE LEFTMOST RIB. That is the whole route-finding instruction and the word that matters is leftmost. Several rib features present themselves at that shelf; the correct one is the far left of them.

ORIENT YOURSELF ON THE FACE AS A WHOLE BEFORE YOU START, BECAUSE IT IS CROWDED: running WEST to EAST across it the order is the Northeast Rib lines, then a route in a vertical cleft with a waterfall, then the Northeast Buttress. The Cascade-Johannesburg couloir is the broad snow line that separates Johannesburg from Cascade Peak, and this route uses it as a stairway rather than climbing it to the col.

AND KNOW WHAT THE COULOIR ITSELF IS: it is the original 1938 line and the most popular one, finishing at the col rather than on any rib. If you are still in the snow at the top, you never left for the rib.

approach_variants.name: Down into the avalanche moat before the couloir narrows, then the left-hand rib
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, July and August, once the rib is snow-free enough to climb but before it goes fully dry and looser
approach_variants.notes:
A quick approach directly from the car, which is the only quick thing about this route. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, descend to and cross the Cascade River, cross the terminal moraine, and gain the couloir apron.

The start is unusual and it is the route's signature: you DOWNCLIMB INTO AN AVALANCHE MOAT to gain the rock, around 4,400 ft, on sketchy lichen-covered dirty slabs.

What follows is honest about itself — initial fourth class into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby horizontal gully traverse of about 60 ft at 5.5 with minimal protection, steep heather taken by finger-pressing rather than by holds, and then roughly 700 ft of genuinely good 5.6 rock leading toward a bivy site near the glacier, two pitches below the summit.

Two starts exist: the original 1951 line, faster but with a scary 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds about 500 ft on more logical terrain to avoid it.
hazards: Extensive loose rock and lichen-slick slabs from the very first moves
Vegetation-dependent, largely unprotectable terrain — the climbing is real but the protection often is not
Icefall and rockfall from the hanging glaciers 5,000 ft above the route
Rockfall on the shared East Ridge and Sill Glacier descent
A descent whose steep heather section is repeatedly named as the most dangerous part of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU GO DOWN TO GET ON. That is the base finding and it is unlike anything else on this side of the mountain: from the moraine you DOWNCLIMB INTO AN AVALANCHE MOAT to reach the rock, at roughly 4,400 ft. If you are stepping up onto rock rather than down into a gap, you have not found the start.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE COULOIR'S SHAPE, AND IT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE VARIATION THAT SHARES ITS NAME: LEAVE THE CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COULOIR BEFORE IT NARROWS. The 1957 variation gains rock HIGHER, close to where the couloir visibly pinches down. IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED THE COULOIR UNTIL IT CONSTRICTS, YOU HAVE PASSED THIS ROUTE'S START.

THEN COUNT THE RIBS, BECAUSE THERE ARE TWO AND THEY ALMOST TOUCH DOWN LOW: two parallel ribs jut off the same buttress. THE 1951 ROUTE TAKES THE LEFT RIB. The 1957 route takes the more prominent RIGHT one. They nearly intersect at the bottom and only diverge as you gain height, which is exactly why the choice has to be made deliberately rather than by following the ground.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS VEGETATION, AND HERE IT IS THE POSITIVE SIGN RATHER THAN THE WARNING: fourth-class ground leads straight into DENSE VERTICAL TREE-ROOT CLIMBING. If you are on clean rock from the start you are not on this rib — the 1963 Northeast Ridge, one line over, is explicitly the route with no bush climbing on it.

AND IF YOU ARE STILL IN SNOW AT THE TOP, you climbed the couloir itself — the 1938 original — which finishes at the Cascade-Johannesburg col and never touches either rib.

approach_variants.name: Kool-Aid Lake side: easy slopes southwest of the peak to the chimney and the notch
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the South Ridge: Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles of switchbacks to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then leave the maintained trail for the Ptarmigan Traverse climbers' path — a rising traverse across Mixup Peak's flanks to the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft and over CACHE COL at about 6,900 ft, then down about 600 ft toward Kool-Aid Lake at roughly 6,200 ft.

From there, rather than dropping all the way to the lake and continuing to the Magic-Hurry-up col, continue onto the easy slopes on Magic Mountain's SOUTHWEST side and up to the base of the ridge and face.

The climbing is short: steep broken rock, then an easy chimney to a notch, then a traverse and a short finish on the northwest face.
hazards: Broken Magic Mountain gneiss with no fixed anchors — a retreat means leaving slings on blocks
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees, going to bare ice with open marginal moats late in the season
An aspect that dries late and stays greasy after rain; wet lichen on gneiss is treacherous on class 4 ground
Almost no traffic, so no bootpack, no cairns and no cleaned-off rock
No cell coverage on a rarely visited side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY NORTHWEST OF THE SUMMIT IS SHARED WITH THE NORTH FACE ROUTE, SO THE NOTCH ALONE CANNOT TELL YOU WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON. WHAT TELLS YOU IS HOW YOU GOT TO IT. This route reaches the notch from EASY WALKING SLOPES ON THE SOUTHWEST SIDE, off the Kool-Aid Lake basin, with no glacier involved. The North Face reaches the same notch from the Yawning Glacier on the far side of the mountain, with a schrund below it. IF YOU CROSSED A GLACIER TO GET WHERE YOU ARE STANDING, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH FACE.

THE SEQUENCE FROM THE BASE IS COUNTABLE AND IT ENDS IN A CHIMNEY: easy slopes to the base, then STEEP BROKEN ROCK, then an EASY CHIMNEY that leads to the notch. Rock first, chimney second, notch third. If you have not climbed a chimney, you have not reached the notch this route uses.

THE OTHER TEST IS WHAT YOU DID NOT CROSS. Two other routes leave from this same southwest side and both are identified by a feature this one lacks. THE WEST RIDGE CROSSES A BERGSCHRUND ON A POCKET GLACIER before it climbs anything — if you crossed a schrund, you are on the West Ridge. THE SOUTHWEST CIRQUE stays in the cirque and goes up HEATHER gullies — if you are on grass rather than rock, you are in the cirque. This route is dry walking, then rock, then a chimney.

AND IF YOU CONTINUED TO THE MAGIC-HURRY-UP COL YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR SOUTH: that col is the start of the South Ridge and of Hurry-Up Peak's own route, on the far side of this basin.

FINISH CHECK: from the notch the summit is a short traverse and climb on the NORTHWEST FACE. If the notch you reached puts the summit a long way off, it is not the right notch.

approach_variants.name: The pocket glacier under the west face, and the schrund that guards it
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with the bergschrund crossing and the pocket-glacier conditions varying by snow year
approach_variants.notes:
Approach by the general Cascade Pass and Ptarmigan Traverse access: Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, the trail to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then the climbers' path across Mixup Peak's flanks, over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col near 6,900 ft, and down toward the Kool-Aid Lake basin.

From the basin, easy slopes on the west-southwest side lead to the small POCKET GLACIER under Magic Mountain's west face. That pocket glacier is the base area, and the bergschrund at its head is where the route begins.

Seven pitches: shelves to a blocky open book, the 5.6 open book, the slab taken on its easier left side, and an easy chimney on the left to gain the crest between the false and main summits.
hazards: A bergschrund below the west face whose difficulty varies by year and which can be the crux of the route by late summer
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees and bare ice late season
Broken gneiss with slung blocks for belays and no fixed gear
A thin slab pitch where protection is limited
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE ROUTE'S IDENTITY AND IT IS THE ONE-LOOK TEST AGAINST BOTH ITS NEIGHBOURS ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. THIS IS THE ONLY MAGIC MOUNTAIN ROUTE FROM THE KOOL-AID LAKE SIDE THAT CROSSES A SCHRUND. The Northwest Ridge walks up easy slopes to rock and a chimney; the Southwest Cirque goes up heather gullies. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A GAP BETWEEN GLACIER AND ROCK, YOU ARE NOT ON THE WEST RIDGE.

THE POSITIVE LANDMARK ABOVE THE SCHRUND IS A NAMED SHAPE: shelves lead up to a BLOCKY OPEN BOOK — a dihedral corner. That open book is the 5.6 crux and the best-protected pitch on the route. IF YOU CROSS THE SCHRUND AND FIND NO OPEN-BOOK CORNER ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE CROSSED IT IN THE WRONG PLACE.

COUNT THE FOUR FEATURES IN ORDER, BECAUSE THEY ARE ALL DIFFERENT SHAPES: schrund, shelves, open book, slab. THE SLAB IS TAKEN ON ITS EASIER LEFT SIDE, not up the middle.

THE FINISH TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE UNDER: from below the ridge between the FALSE and MAIN summits, an easy chimney on the LEFT gains the crest. So the route deliberately arrives on the ridge BETWEEN the two tops — if the chimney you climbed put you straight onto a summit, you are on the false one and the ridge continues.

AND THE SCHRUND HAS TO WORK IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: the descent reverses the chimney and slab, downclimbs the open book and re-crosses the schrund. Look at it on the way up with that in mind, because there is no walk-off from this side.

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier, then west across the glacier head to the face
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug; glacier cover and couloir conditions vary more year to year here than on the peak's south side
approach_variants.notes:
This route and the Northeast Couloir come at the mountain from the OTHER side to everything else on it. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then cross the pass and descend east toward the Stehekin side. Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the YAWNING GLACIER, which runs roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft. Rope up. Follow the glacier southwest to the MAGIC-PELTON COL at 6,480 ft, between Magic Mountain and Pelton Peak.

From the col this route does not go straight up. It bears back and crosses the HEAD of the glacier westward to reach the north face, where about 600 ft of steep class 4 rock leads to a notch immediately northwest of the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Yawning Glacier — rope up rather than treating it as a snowfield
A steep couloir below the Magic-Pelton col that is exposed to rockfall
A schrund at the base of the rock that opens through the season and can be the crux by August
Broken, north-facing gneiss that is often wet or verglassed, with slung blocks for anchors and no fixed gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO ROUTES LEAVE THE MAGIC-PELTON COL AND THE TEST IS WHETHER YOU WALK OR TRAVERSE. At the col at 6,480 ft, THE NORTHEAST COULOIR GOES STRAIGHT UP FROM WHERE YOU STAND. THIS ROUTE FIRST BEARS BACK AND CROSSES THE HEAD OF THE GLACIER TO THE WEST. IF YOU STARTED CLIMBING AT THE COL, YOU ARE IN THE COULOIR.

THE SECOND TEST IS WHAT IS UNDER YOUR HANDS, AND IT SETTLES THE SAME PAIR FROM THE OTHER END: this route is ROCK — about 600 ft of steep class 4 above a schrund. The Northeast Couloir is SNOW, 40 to 50 degrees for 2,000 ft. IF YOU ARE PLACING PICKETS YOU ARE IN THE COULOIR; IF YOU ARE SLINGING BLOCKS YOU ARE ON THE FACE.

THE SCHRUND AT THE BASE OF THE ROCK IS THE BASE ITSELF, and it is the thing that changes most between June and August — by late summer it can be the hardest move of the day.

THE FINISH IS A NOTCH IMMEDIATELY NORTHWEST OF THE SUMMIT, AND THAT NOTCH IS SHARED WITH THE NORTHWEST RIDGE, which reaches it from the peak's southwest side by easy walking slopes and a chimney. So arriving at the notch does not confirm which route you climbed — but it does confirm you are 600 ft above the glacier on the correct face, and the summit is a short scramble from there.

AND YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN ENTIRELY IF YOU CAME OVER CACHE COL: that is the Kool-Aid Lake approach, which serves the South Ridge, the West Ridge, the Northwest Ridge and the Southwest Cirque. This route and the Northeast Couloir come from Pelton Basin.

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier to the col, then straight up the line
approach_variants.season: April to late June or early July as a snow line, but the road is the constraint: Cascade River Road usually does not open to the Cascade Pass trailhead until the end of June, so a spring ascent means a long road walk or ski from the gate, commonly starting at the Eldorado parking area. In practice late June and early July is the sweet spot, when the road opens and the couloir is still full
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, cross it and descend east toward the Stehekin side; Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass, 4.9 miles and 1,800 ft from the trailhead including the camp spur.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the YAWNING GLACIER, rope up, and follow the glacier southwest to the MAGIC-PELTON COL at 6,480 ft. Ski parties also reach this cirque from the Cascade Pass side across the Yawning Glacier without dropping to Pelton Basin.

Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir: roughly 2,000 ft winding down the shoulder, a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 at the very top.

Decide your descent BEFORE you leave the col. Reversing the couloir is direct but puts you in a sun-exposed funnel; walking off the South Ridge to the Magic-Hurry-up col and Kool-Aid Lake avoids it entirely but lands you on the opposite side of the mountain.
hazards: Cliff faces on both sides funnel rockfall down the line — one report calls the lower section potentially a bit of a garbage chute
Documented significant sluffing on spring snow, with large natural avalanches reported in the same zone later the same day
An upper couloir sustaining 45-50 degrees and reaching a proper 50 at the top, often a firm crust under a few inches of new snow
A crevassed Yawning Glacier on the approach and a sun-facing couloir below it, which shortens the descent window
Overhead hazard for the full length of the line
A cornice on the summit ridge in spring
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT THE MAGIC-PELTON COL AT 6,480 FT, THE COULOIR RISES DIRECTLY ABOVE YOU. THAT IS THE TEST: THE LINE STARTS AT THE COL, WITHOUT A TRAVERSE. If your next move after reaching the col is to bear back west across the head of the glacier, you are heading for the North Face — a rock route on the same mountain from the same col.

SO: PICKETS AND FRONT POINTS MEAN YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT PLACE. This is snow, 40-45 degrees low down and 45-50 above, for about 2,000 ft. If you are slinging blocks and climbing class 4 rock, you have traversed onto the North Face.

THE SHAPE OF THE LINE IS THE CONFIRMATION: consistently steep but WIDE, with rock faces on BOTH sides that shed into the gut. A narrow slot, or an open face with no walls beside it, is not this feature. Move through the lower section rather than resting in it — those walls are what make it a funnel.

BE AWARE THAT MORE THAN ONE NORTHEAST-FACING LINE IS DESCRIBED ON THIS MOUNTAIN AND THE PUBLISHED ACCOUNTS DO NOT FULLY AGREE ON WHICH IS WHICH. One is reached from a col on the northwest shoulder, one from a col named Alliteration Col, and one from the Magic-Pelton col — and at least one account treats two of these as different lines. The col you stand at is what identifies your line, not the couloir seen from below, so record which col you crossed and how high it was.

AND THE SEASON IS A CHECK IN ITSELF: this is a snow route. The guidebook allows for rock or snow depending on the year, but if you have arrived to find loose rock rather than a filled line, the couloir is out of condition and it is the same funnel with nothing holding it together.

approach_variants.name: Bivy at the C-J col, then across the moat onto the peak's northwest side
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the moat below the northwest side is crossable — the one documented ascent is a July trip
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as the East Ridge: Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass trailhead, the Cascade Pass trail to the pass at 5,392 ft, then cross-country by way of Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier to the CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COL. The col sits directly between Cascade Peak and Johannesburg Mountain, and it is the staging point.

From a bivy at the col, cross the moat below Cascade Peak's northwest side to reach the base of the route. One documented party started up around 9 a.m. the morning after bivying at the col.

Three pitches. This route sees so few ascents that it should be treated as an unmaintained line rather than a climb with beta: the 2013 party found NO rappel anchors, NO pitons and NO summit register, and rated the crux first pitch nearer 5.10 than the guidebook's 5.8 because of the loose rock.

Budget for building every anchor from scratch on the way down. That party's descent from the summit to the col took about four and a half hours.
hazards: Extreme rockfall and loose rock on all three pitches
No fixed protection and no fixed anchors anywhere on the route — natural placements are the norm and can be poor
A moat below the northwest side that is the gate on the whole climb
So few ascents that neither conditions nor anchors can be assumed to be in place
A first pitch that has been found two grades harder than its guidebook rating
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ABSENCE OF FIXED GEAR IS THE CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS AN UNUSUALLY RELIABLE ONE HERE. A 2013 party climbing this route found no rappel anchors, no pitons and no summit register on the entire peak. IF YOU ARRIVE AT A BASE WITH TAT, BOLTS OR A WORN START, YOU ARE NOT ON THE NORTHWEST CHIMNEY — everything around Cascade Pass that sees traffic shows it, and this does not.

THE BASE IS ACROSS A MOAT FROM THE CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COL. You do not walk to it: from the col you cross the gap where the snow has pulled back from the peak's northwest side, and the route starts on the rock beyond. The col itself is unmistakable — it is the notch between Cascade Peak and Johannesburg, and it is where the C-J couloir tops out.

COUNT THREE PITCHES AND EXPECT THE MIDDLE ONE TO BE THE SHAPE THE ROUTE IS NAMED FOR: a broken, loose crack pitch first; then the CHIMNEY — aesthetic, sparsely protected, and wanting a large offset or Big Bro-style cam; then very loose fifth-class ground simul-climbed from a FALSE SUMMIT to the true summit. If there is no chimney on your second pitch, the line is wrong.

AND THE FALSE SUMMIT IS PART OF THE ROUTE, NOT AN ERROR: the third pitch runs from it to the true top. Stopping at the first high point is stopping one pitch short.

WHAT IS HONESTLY THIN HERE: beyond the guidebook entry and that single 2013 trip report there is essentially no published description of this line, and no elevation is recorded for its base. The col and the moat are what can be navigated to; everything above is the party's own route-finding.

approach_variants.name: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, then the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July and wants an axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road — the upper gravel section is gated and often does not open until late June or July — follow the well-graded Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low down, so fill up before the switchbacks.

At the pass leave the maintained tread for the climbers' path heading south-southeast, a rising traverse across snow or heather on Mixup Peak's flanks to the base of the CACHE GLACIER near 6,000 ft. Ascend moderate glacier and snow slopes to CACHE COL at about 6,900 ft. From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock and heather benches to KOOL-AID LAKE at about 6,200 ft — the standard camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water in the basin.

From camp the peak is a side trip: up toward the south flank, across a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft, then broken granite slabs to the ridge. About a mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly an hour to an hour and a half for a fit party.
hazards: Crevasses and snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
Icy, steep snow on the Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake descent, worse refrozen in the early morning or late in the day
A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft that wants an axe and crampons even mid-summer
Loose rock and multiple similar-looking gully lines on the granite benches — the main route-finding crux
Short but exposed moves along the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE COL BETWEEN MAGIC MOUNTAIN AND HURRY-UP PEAK, gained from the Kool-Aid Lake basin, and the col is the last unambiguous feature of the day. Above it the route is route-finding rather than following a line: parties report several viable gully options through the granite benches and not all of them match the guidebook.

SO THE TEST THAT MATTERS IS AT THE TOP, NOT THE BOTTOM, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE. YOU WILL REACH A FALSE SUMMIT. FROM IT YOU MUST DROP ABOUT 80 FT INTO A DIRTY GULLY ON THE RIGHT-HAND (EAST) SIDE, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that CORKSCREW AROUND THE EAST SIDE of the summit block, and the last 50 ft gains the true top. IF YOU HAVE NOT LOST 80 FT INTO A GULLY, THE HIGH POINT YOU ARE STANDING ON IS THE FALSE SUMMIT.

THAT DESCEND-THEN-CORKSCREW SEQUENCE IS THE ROUTE'S SIGNATURE. A summit reached directly off the ridge crest with no drop and no wrap-around is the wrong one.

ON THE WAY UP, THE STEEP SNOW BAND AROUND 7,100 FT IS THE POSITION CHECK: it sits between camp and the slabs, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 3 scramble. If you gained the ridge without crossing snow, look again at where you left the basin.

AND DO NOT CONFUSE THE COL WITH CACHE COL. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier. The Magic-Hurry-up col is on the far side of Kool-Aid Lake and is where this climb starts. Two cols, a mile and a descent apart.

The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a source describing 'the saddle between Magic and S Mountains' is describing this same col.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
approach_variants.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the BOSTON BASIN trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward SHARKFIN COL rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the BOSTON GLACIER. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse SOUTH toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BERGSCHRUND AT THE TOE OF THE FACE, ON THE BOSTON GLACIER, AND THE POSITION TEST IS DIRECTIONAL: from the col you traverse SOUTH across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

THE ENTRY MOVE IS A ZIG-ZAG AND IT IS THE POSITIVE TEST: WORK CLIMBER'S LEFT OF THE BERGSCHRUND, THEN BACK RIGHT INTO THE CENTRE OF THE LOWER FACE, AND THEN STRAIGHT UP. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

WHAT YOU ARE CLIMBING CONFIRMS IT: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

THE FINISH IS THE OTHER COUNTABLE POINT, AND GETTING IT WRONG COSTS TIME AT THE WORST MOMENT: continue straight up until UPPER ROCK CLIFFS force a rising traverse to the LEFT. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, GO LEFT AROUND A CRAGGY ROCK OUTCROP at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

AND THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THIS PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. IF YOU WALKED PAST AN OLD MINE IN A BASIN AT 7,000 FT, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTHWEST ROUTE.

approach_variants.name: Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin to the cowskull snowfield
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road. The maintained Cascade Pass trail switchbacks through old growth and traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at 5,400 ft, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft. From the pass take the Sahale Arm trail north through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier and SAHALE GLACIER CAMP near 7,600 ft — 5.9 miles and about 3,940 ft from the trailhead, and the standard base. NPS permit and bear canister required; camp only in the designated sites. Sahale Arm above the meadows is dry, so carry water or a filter.

From camp the route goes off-trail and DOWNHILL first: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then a short class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft, and traverse roughly two miles across HORSESHOE BASIN on talus, slabs and lingering snow, passing near the old DAVENPORT MINE around 7,000 ft, to reach the base of the southwest face.

Most parties take two to three days for the roughly 20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
hazards: A steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be downclimbed, exposed and fall-prone on firm early-season snow
Rockfall across the Horseshoe Basin traverse, which is loose and easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands below the basin ledge system — stay on the mid-elevation line rather than dropping
Steep snow on the cowskull with wet-slide potential in the afternoon; many parties run a picket belay
Loose scree and rubble above the snow, all the way to the summit ridge
An axe and crampons needed for steep snow patches into midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE HAS A LANDMARK YOU CANNOT MISTAKE FOR ANYTHING ELSE, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS FACE IS NAVIGABLE AT ALL: A DISTINCTIVE COWSKULL-SHAPED SNOWFIELD HIGH ON THE FACE. Climbers describe it as looking like a ghost early in the season. Steepening southwest-facing snowfields lead to a snow chute and then to the cowskull itself, and if you cannot pick a cowskull out of the snow above you, you are under the wrong part of the face.

THE MID-APPROACH CHECKPOINT IS THE DAVENPORT MINE, around 7,000 ft, roughly midway across the Horseshoe Basin traverse. The ruins are unambiguous. If you have crossed the basin without passing old mine workings, you are on the wrong ledge line — and the ones below cliff out.

AND THE APPROACH BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, WHICH IS THE FIRST SANITY CHECK OF THE DAY: from Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 ft you descend Sahale's south ridge and a class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft before you traverse. If you have been climbing since camp, you have not started the route yet.

ABOVE THE COWSKULL, THE GROUND CHANGES CHARACTER AND THAT IS THE SIGNAL TO PUT THE CRAMPONS AWAY: step off the snow, then grovel up loose scree and rubble to the summit ridge, finishing with about 100 ft of class 2-3 rock. Snow the whole way to the top is not this route.

KNOW WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE AIMING FOR: Buckner has two nearly equal tops, the southwest at about 9,114 ft and the northeast about two feet lower, separated by a few hundred feet of ridge. This route reaches the SOUTHWEST one, which is the accepted high point; the northeast top needs the connecting ridge.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE NORTH FACE IS THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN: that route comes from Boston Basin, over Sharkfin Col and across the Boston Glacier, on the opposite side. If you rappelled off a col onto a glacier this morning, you are on the north side.

approach_variants.name: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
approach_variants.season: Mid to late July through September. The moat crossing is easiest once the glacier has receded, around the third week of July, and gets harder again as the season goes on
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead off SR-20 near Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound about ten miles, losing steadily along Bridge Creek, to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp. Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail and head upstream; it gets brushier and less maintained the further you go, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek.

Around mile 13-14 the maintained tread effectively ends. Ford the North Fork — cold and sometimes knee deep, and easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn — then work up scree and third-class slabs on CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the large waterfall draining toward the Goode Glacier, which is the way to avoid the worst brush. Look for the alder tunnel: a boot-path corridor through the slide alder that saves a great deal of thrashing.

Camp around the glacier toe at roughly 5,400-6,800 ft depending on how far you push. Plan on three to four days round trip.
hazards: A moat and bergschrund at the toe of the buttress with a steep step of about 50 degrees where the route steps off the Goode Glacier onto rock — worse as the season goes on, and reported by some parties as impassable late
Open crevasses and overhead serac hazard on the Goode Glacier
Loose and wet rock on the approach slabs beside the waterfall
Cornices on the approach in early season
A route that is difficult to retreat from once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window
A descent by the Southwest Couloir that several parties report taking 8-10 hours from summit to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LANDMARK IS A COLOUR: THE RED LEDGES AT THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS. Three independent accounts name them, and one quotes the guidebook doing so. You are looking for a band of RED ROCK where the Goode Glacier meets the foot of the buttress. If the rock in front of you is grey, keep looking along the toe.

THE BASE IS THE MOAT AT THOSE LEDGES, AND HOW YOU CROSS IT IS THE MEASURE OF THE SEASON: a collapsed or intact snow bridge, a jump, a downclimb, or a short rappel followed by re-climbing on the far side. Published elevations for this point range from about 6,400 to 7,800 ft across different years and different parties, which is a real disagreement rather than a single number — the glacier has retreated and the crossing point moves. NAVIGATE TO THE RED LEDGES, NOT TO AN ALTITUDE.

ABOVE THE MOAT, EXPECT ONE OR TWO PITCHES OF LOW FIFTH ON PRECARIOUS BLOCKS, TRENDING CLIMBER'S RIGHT to gain the buttress crest proper. If your first ground above the glacier is clean and solid, you are not on the toe.

TELL IT FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER LONG ROUTE BY WHETHER YOU EVER TOUCHED THE GLACIER: MEGALODON RIDGE IS GAINED FROM THE EAST WITHOUT CROSSING THE GOODE GLACIER AT ALL. If you crossed a moat off glacier ice, you are on the Northeast Buttress. If you never left brush and rock, you are on Megalodon.

CONFIRM AS YOU CLIMB: over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class on the crest, often soloed or simul-climbed, then around 8,000 ft a short UNPROTECTABLE 5.7 SLAB on the crest that most parties deviate RIGHT to avoid, then roughly five pitches of 5.4-5.5 easing toward the summit. A route that is hard from the bottom is not this one.

approach_variants.name: Off the Bridge Creek trail to the toe of the arete descending northeast off the main ridge
approach_variants.season: Late summer, August into September, once the approach bushwhack and the glacier are most passable; a long committing route that wants a stable weather window
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead near 4,800 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

WHERE TO LEAVE THE TRAIL IS DISPUTED AND BOTH VERSIONS ARE RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN AVERAGED. The first-ascent account describes leaving at an obvious CLEARING BEFORE GRIZZLY CREEK and climbing from there to the toe of the arete. The route's own catalog description instead has the party continue past Grizzly Creek to around trail-mile 14, ford the North Fork, work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall, and then commit to a steep sustained bushwhack through slide alder and timber for roughly the last half mile.

Either way the objective is the same feature and the total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.
hazards: Hidden cliff bands inside the brush and loose footing on the slabs beside the waterfall
A very long sustained ridge — 2,800 to 3,000 ft of climbing with about 5,000 ft of exposure on one side and 4,000 on the other
Mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches, so long sections carry limited protection
Very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are both thin
Benightment on the ridge is a real risk, and the standard descent drops into the Park Creek drainage on the far side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FEATURE IS A CLEAN-LOOKING ARETE THAT DESCENDS NORTHEAST OFF THE MAIN RIDGE, AND YOU AIM FOR ITS TOE. That is what both accounts of this route agree on. It sits close beneath the Goode Glacier's lower icefall — near it, not on it.

THE SINGLE STRONGEST TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER CROSS THE GLACIER. The Northeast Buttress, the peak's other big route on this side, is reached by stepping off the Goode Glacier across a moat at a band of red rock. THIS ROUTE IS GAINED FROM THE EAST, FROM BRUSH AND ROCK, WITH NO GLACIER CROSSING AT ALL. If you have crampons on to reach your base, you are on the Buttress.

THE ARETE ANNOUNCES ITSELF BY BEING CLEAN. It is described as a clean-looking arete precisely because the ground around it is not — the last half mile of approach is slide alder and timber. Emerging from brush onto a distinct clean crest running down to the northeast is the confirmation.

COUNT THE FIRST STAGE: simul-climbing up the lower arete to a TOWER AT ABOUT 8,200 FT, then ONE RAPPEL off it, and only then running-belay climbing along the crest toward the southeast peak. A rappel early on a ridge you are ascending is a strong positional marker and it is the first one this route gives you.

THE CRUX IS LATE AND IT IS ABOVE THE GLACIER: three long pitches of 5.9-5.10 on the southeast peak headwall, with easier options further left, and then an overhanging 5.10 headwall above the Goode Glacier near Black Tooth Notch with an icy moat to negotiate. If you have met your hardest climbing in the first half of the day, you are on something else.

approach_variants.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
approach_variants.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,875 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 2,000 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ENTRY IS MARKED: A NARROW LEDGE WITH A CAIRN ON IT LEADS INTO THE SOUTHWEST GULLY. After skirting snow you scramble talus and loose scree to that ledge. A cairn on a narrow ledge is the confirmation; an unmarked scramble straight into a gully is not this entry.

INSIDE THE GULLY THE TEST IS COLOUR, AND IT IS BOTH A ROUTE-FINDING AND A SAFETY INSTRUCTION: HUG THE LEFT SIDE, WHERE THE DARK ROCK IS SOLID. Parties call that band the black stairs and it offers cleaner scrambling than the middle of the gully. IF YOU ARE ON PALE, RUBBLY ROCK, YOU ARE IN THE GUT OF THE COULOIR AND ON THE LOOSE LINE.

EXPECT ONE SHORT LOW-FIFTH PITCH LOW DOWN, then class 3 and 4 in the main gully, steepening near the notch between the summit and the West Tower.

BLACK TOOTH NOTCH IS THE UPPER LANDMARK AND IT IS SHARED, SO IT IDENTIFIES THE MOUNTAIN RATHER THAN THE ROUTE: a foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse, with a fixed sling marking the crux step, and loose rock throughout. The Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge both DESCEND through it; this is the only one of the three that climbs UP through it.

AND THE MOST USEFUL NEGATIVE FACT IS ABOUT GOING DOWN, BECAUSE THAT IS WHEN IT BITES: the couloir's mouth opens onto cliffs above a WATERFALL. EXIT LEFT ONTO EASIER HEATHER BENCHES rather than continuing straight down. A party that is still descending the fall line when it hears water below has gone too far.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, the Douglas Creek alder, then the west-side gully to the polished slabs
approach_variants.season: June and July for the best glacier conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 151, about 3,700 ft. Hike 3.5 miles and 2,800 ft to Easy Pass at 6,500 ft, then descend 1.5 miles through alpine meadows and forest into Fisher Basin and down to the Fisher Creek valley floor and the established campsites.

Cross Fisher Creek on a large fallen log and travel the east side of the Douglas Creek valley on a faint climbers' path. THIS IS WHERE THE ROUTE IS ACTUALLY DECIDED. The transition from forest to open terrain runs into a vast field of slide alder and brush over ten feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, cut by small rocky stream channels — progress measured in inches per minute. One 2022 party was turned back at 4,200 ft by this alone, having covered half a mile an hour for seven hours. One account rates the route five stars for glacier travel and one star for the bushwhack, which is fair.

Above the brush, the way onto the glacier is a gully on the west side of the basin. Then it is glacier travel to the col and a short summit block.
hazards: A slide-alder thicket over ten feet high that has defeated at least one party outright, with heavy mosquito and black-fly pressure
Cliff bands ringing the Fisher Basin cirque
Crevasses and glide cracks reported over 20 ft deep on the Douglas Glacier
A steep, exposed rock ramp of roughly 300 ft above camp that is hard to protect
Steep icy summit snow needing solid crampon and axe technique
Steep loose-rock switchbacks on the Easy Pass trail itself above mile 2.5
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS ON THE WEST SIDE OF THE BASIN AND IT IS IDENTIFIED BY WHAT IT DELIVERS YOU ONTO, NOT BY ITS ENTRANCE. It starts class 3, steepens quickly to class 4 or low fifth for a short section that is hard to protect, and TOPS OUT ON GLACIER-POLISHED SLABS. Polished slabs above a short steep step is the confirmation. From there it is about 1,500 vertical ft of scrambling on those slabs to the TOE OF THE DOUGLAS GLACIER.

SO THE ORDER IS: BRUSH, GULLY, POLISHED SLABS, GLACIER. If you are on slabs without having climbed a short hard step, you have not been through the gully.

THE ROUTE JOINS ITS NEIGHBOUR NEAR THE TOP AND THAT IS EXPECTED: ascend the Douglas Glacier — steep at its head — to the COL, then traverse to meet the BANDED GLACIER and finish up the same class 3-4 summit block, about 300 vertical ft. A summit block reached without crossing to a second glacier means you are still on the Douglas side of the col.

THE APPROACH IS THE STRONGEST DISCRIMINATOR ON THIS MOUNTAIN, BECAUSE ALL THREE ROUTES END AT THE SAME SUMMIT BUT NONE OF THEM SHARE A VALLEY. This route comes from EASY PASS and the DOUGLAS CREEK drainage on the west. The Banded Glacier comes from Fisher Creek to a lake camp at 5,160 ft and crosses a col onto the Banded. The Fremont Glacier comes from Thunder Creek and PARK CREEK PASS on the southeast. If you passed Park Creek Pass this morning, you are not on the Douglas.

AND THE HONEST GAP: no source publishes a countable marker for the gully entrance itself — it is described only as being on the west side of the basin. The polished slabs above it are the reliable confirmation, which means you find out you were right after the hard part.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
approach_variants.season: July and August
approach_variants.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail north for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually NORTHWARD around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the FREMONT GLACIER SADDLE around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present — rope up
A bergschrund that opens below the summit ridge as the snow finger melts out late season, and a moat where the glacier meets the crest
Exposed, often unroped class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Footlog crossings over Thunder and Park creeks that are hazardous at night or in high water
No fixed anchors anywhere on the route — a rappel off the summit block has to be built from a horn, a chockstone or a picket
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE HOGSBACK — the snow spine at the UPPER edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a MOAT CROSSING to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

THEN COUNT THREE FEATURES IN ORDER, AND THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM: a class 3-4 ROCK PITCH gains a LEFT-SLANTING RAMP — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 LEDGES ON THE EAST SIDE of the ridge lead through a U-NOTCH between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS THE RAMP: IF YOU ARE TRYING TO CLIMB THE SUMMIT TOWER DIRECTLY FROM THE GLACIER, YOU HAVE MISSED IT. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants LEFT. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

THE U-NOTCH IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION AND IT IS A SHAPE, NOT A HEIGHT: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's EAST flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

AND KNOW WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON BEFORE YOU START: this is the SOUTHEAST/SOUTHWEST approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the west; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Creek to the lake camp, over the ridge onto the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.season: June and July
approach_variants.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — some accounts call it Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the BANDED GLACIER on the far side and ascend it to the BANDED-DOUGLAS COL.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: A major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier
Talus lying on top of bullet-hard glacier ice, described as a pile of marbles — treacherous in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp
Loose chossy rock on the summit ridge and rockfall in the approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CRITICAL TRANSITION IS NAMED IN THE ROUTE'S OWN DESCRIPTION AND IT IS A NEGATIVE TEST: GAIN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE ON SOLID ROCK AT ABOUT 8,800 FT RATHER THAN ATTEMPTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK DIRECTLY FROM THE GLACIER. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

GETTING THERE IS A SEQUENCE OF TWO COLS AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT THINGS. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE — recorded in one account as Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the BANDED-DOUGLAS COL, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to REACH ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

SO THE QUESTION THAT SETTLES YOUR POSITION IN FOG IS WHICH GLACIER IS UNDER YOU: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

AND ALL THREE LOGAN ROUTES END ON THE SAME 300 FT OF CLASS 3-4 SUMMIT BLOCK, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from FISHER CREEK and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

WATCH THE SCREE BELOW THE GLACIER ON THE WAY UP with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass, the sandy gully and the rocky point, then up to the Booker-Buckner col
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, when the snowbridges near the Booker-Buckner col are still intact but consolidated. Conditions change year to year and can degrade within days
approach_variants.notes:
The usual approach is a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass — on the order of forty miles round trip with roughly 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — or as a leg of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass, Buckner and Park Creek Pass.

From a camp near Park Creek Pass, this is a short day. Hike about 0.4 mile north on the Thunder Creek trail, pick up the climber's track, and traverse northeast: cross a BROAD SANDY GULLY at about 6,900 ft, roughly a mile from the pass, continue toward a SHARP ROCKY POINT at about 7,760 ft, then turn RIGHT and uphill on talus and snow to the col and its small glacier.

The col is around 8,100 ft and the scramble above it is class 2-3 with no technical rock. Booker sees roughly one party a year, so expect no boot track and no cairns.
hazards: Crevasses and a bergschrund at the Booker-Buckner col, bypassed only on snowbridges of variable reliability — one such bridge collapsed within a week of another party crossing it, with climbers on both sides
Loose blocks in the summit gully, with rockfall released by climbers above as the route's principal hazard
Slick meltwater-run rock slabs for parties coming in from the Horseshoe Basin side
A remote, multi-day position far from any road or quick rescue
No boot track and no cairns — the route is walked by about one party a year
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS NAVIGATED BY A CHAIN OF THREE POSITIONS RATHER THAN ONE LANDMARK, AND THE CHAIN IS COUNTABLE IN FOG: A BROAD SANDY GULLY AT ABOUT 6,900 FT, roughly a mile from Park Creek Pass. Then a SHARP, ROCKY POINT AT ABOUT 7,760 FT. Then TURN RIGHT AND UPHILL to the col. Miss the gully and you are too low; pass the rocky point without turning and you are traversing past the peak.

THE BASE IS THE BOOKER-BUCKNER COL AT ABOUT 8,100 FT, and it is the col rather than the summit that the whole day is about: the upper snow and the glacier margin below it hold the crevasses, and the same snowbridges have to work on the way back down. Sound them, cross early while frozen, and note where you crossed.

ABOVE THE COL, A NORTH-FACING GULLY LEADS TOWARD THE SUMMIT WITH ONE SHORT CLASS 3 STEP. Keep to one side of it rather than the gut, and do not stack the party one above another.

THE ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS AT THE TOP AND IT IS SPECIFIC: LEAVING THE GULLY TOO EARLY PUTS YOU ABOVE A SHORT WALL ON THE WEST, and forces an awkward traverse back on small ledges. Cut RIGHT out of the gully onto low-angle talus and scree, and walk those to the summit. If you find yourself edging along small ledges above a wall, you exited one notch too soon.

TELL IT FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER WALK-UP BY HEIGHT: the South Ridge is gained across Horseshoe Basin at a permanent snowfield around 7,000-7,200 ft and trends to the ridge WEST of the summit. This route goes a thousand feet higher, to the col between Booker and Buckner. If you never got above 7,500 ft before starting to climb, you are on the South Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
approach_variants.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
approach_variants.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend LEFT up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse RIGHT through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
hazards: An icefall traversed on the approach, with crevasse and serac fall the standing hazard and the crossing itself described as frightening
A crumbly red rock stratum crossing the whole face at mid-height, which is where the rockfall comes from
Extreme remoteness — an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed would be very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground, which the first-ascent account flags as compounding the difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SEQUENCE IS COUNTABLE FROM BOTTOM TO TOP AND IT IS THE BEST THING THIS ROUTE HAS: EASIER CLIFFS, THEN A SMALL GLACIER, THEN LEFT UP IT TO AN ICEFALL, THEN RIGHT THROUGH THE ICEFALL TO THE ROCK. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one.

THE ROPE-UP POINT IS A LEDGE SYSTEM NEAR THE SECOND PROMINENT TREE, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible.

THE MID-ROUTE CONFIRMATION IS A COLOUR AND IT CROSSES THE WHOLE FACE: a PROMINENT, CRUMBLY RED STRATUM at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting.

BETWEEN THOSE TWO, FOLLOW THE PROMINENT CENTRAL RIB essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-FT NOTCH is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE WHOLE PEAK: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

approach_variants.name: Horseshoe Basin at 6,400-6,600 ft to the north-facing gully and the permanent snowfield
approach_variants.season: July through September, after Cascade River Road opens and once Horseshoe Basin's snowfields have consolidated; early attempts face more snow travel and less obvious route-finding, late ones find slopes melted to loose scree and slab
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike the Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then continue up the Sahale Arm trail toward Sahale Glacier and Sahale Camp.

Leave the maintained trail near Sahale Camp and descend cross-country into Horseshoe Basin by a snow-free gully on Sahale's south side around 6,600 ft. Traverse the basin staying roughly between 6,400 and 6,600 ft, past the Buckner buttress.

Most parties combine Booker with Buckner on the same trip, since both share this approach and this traverse. Route-finding through Horseshoe Basin is the crux of the day; the climbing is not.
hazards: Loose scree and slabby terrain throughout Horseshoe Basin, easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands flanking the south ridge that have to be route-found around
Rockfall potential in the gullies flanking the ridge
A remote position with no cell coverage and very infrequent traffic if a rescue is needed
A cross-country traverse and an exposed summit gully that are far more hazardous to reverse in the dark or after a thunderstorm has softened the snowfields
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NORTH-FACING ROCK GULLY AND A PERMANENT SNOWFIELD AT ABOUT 7,000-7,200 FT, reached by crossing Horseshoe Basin rather than by climbing to any col. The snowfield is the marker: it is permanent, so it is there whatever the month, and the gully leads off it to the south-trending ridge WEST of Booker's summit.

THE HEIGHT IS THE TEST THAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM ITS NEIGHBOUR, AND IT IS A THOUSAND FEET WIDE. The Northwest Route starts at the BOOKER-BUCKNER COL at about 8,100 ft, reached from Park Creek Pass by way of a sandy gully at 6,900 ft and a sharp rocky point at 7,760 ft. THIS ROUTE STARTS A THOUSAND FEET LOWER AND ON THE OTHER SIDE. If you are standing at a col between two peaks, you are not on the South Ridge.

THE APPROACH TEST IS THAT YOU GO DOWN BEFORE YOU GO UP: from Sahale Camp you descend Sahale's south side through a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin and traverse at 6,400-6,600 ft. If your day has been a continuous climb from the trailhead, you have not reached the basin traverse yet.

THE FINISH IS SHORT AND EXPOSED AND IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF REAL CLIMBING: talus and slabs give way to a short, somewhat exposed 3rd-class gully or dike — locally described as taking a 4th-class step — to the summit.

WHAT IS HONESTLY THIN HERE: this ridge is barely documented. The only outside mention found is of a party who ABANDONED the South Ridge for loose terrain and moved to the Northwest Route, finding existing rappel slings on the ridge — which suggests it is sometimes retreated from rather than climbed. Treat the snowfield and the gully as the navigation and expect to do your own route-finding above them.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and about two miles up to Two Mile Camp and the switchbacks to PARK CREEK PASS. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles up the trail, five minutes further into the woods.

From Park Creek Pass, leave the maintained trail and traverse cross-country west-southwest across snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
hazards: Loose blocky rock on the talus approach and the summit ridge, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and ice in the basin and the summit gully into early August, and bullet-hard patches
An exposed class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
In-situ slings at the crux that are aging tat and need backing up before they are weighted
Extreme remoteness — assume a multi-day evacuation or a helicopter for any serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT THIS APPROACH IS THAT BELOW 7,400 FT IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM GOODE MOUNTAIN'S. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE NOTCH, AND THE WORD IS RIGHT-MOST. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the RIGHT-MOST one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

CROSS TO THE NORTH SIDE OF THAT NOTCH AND THE GROUND CHANGES CHARACTER COMPLETELY: a fun ledge traverse on the BACKSIDE of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED TO THE NORTH SIDE, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE LEDGE TRAVERSE, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

CONFIRM ON THE LEDGE: it includes a SQUEEZE UNDER A SLIGHT OVERHANG, and there are IN-SITU SLINGS at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

THE LAST MOVE IS A CHOICE, NOT A CRUX: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its LEFT side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

AND KNOW WHICH TOP YOU WANT: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the EASTERNMOST is the true high point.

_SKIPPED._note: Nine routes with an empty approach_variants were deliberately left empty. An empty result is a real result; each reason below is a statement about what is published or about what the row IS, not about effort.
_SKIPPED.wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges: NOT AN ASCENT LINE. The row's own approach says it in as many words: reached only from the summit of Forbidden after climbing another route, with no independent trailhead approach, since it is used almost exclusively as a descent. Its base is a horn near the summit. Writing a base finding would mean inventing a way to arrive at something you can only leave from. The Ledges are named as a NEGATIVE test inside the East Ridge Direct and Northeast Face entries instead, which is where a party is actually at risk of confusing them.
_SKIPPED.wa_northwest_ridge_2: POSITIONED ONLY RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOUR, AND THE ROW SAYS SO ITSELF. Boston Peak's Northwest Ridge has one recorded ascent — a leg of a 2018 traverse of the whole Boston Basin rim — and that party reached it by climbing Sharkfin Tower, descending from it, and traversing a steep hanging snow slope to the base of the crest. There is no independent approach to the foot of the ridge. The row's own approach paragraph is explicitly labelled a reasoned estimate from the area's standard access pattern rather than documented beta, and independent searching of Mountain Project, SummitPost, CascadeClimbers, Mountaineers.org, WTA and the AAC turned up no pitch-level description. 'The base of the ridge, at the bottom of a snow traverse from another summit' is not a fog test.
_SKIPPED.wa_austera_peak_chockstone_route: IT IS THE TOP PITCH OF THE STANDARD ROUTE, NOT A ROUTE WITH ITS OWN BASE. The chockstone chimney is roughly 60 ft at 5.2 and sits in the gully directly below the notch between Austera's false and true summits — the guidebook frames it as one of two ways to reach that notch, the other being an exposed class 3-4 scramble round to the east. Its approach is the same glacier traverse, the same Klawatti-Austera notch and the same 75 ft rappel as wa_austera_peak_southwest_ridge, which already carries the chimney as its third pitch. Writing this row would put a second base finding on the same 60 ft of chimney. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_south_ridge_6: UNDER-PUBLISHED, AND ITS OWN ROW IS PARTLY BORROWED PROSE. The Aiguille de l'M's South Ridge has a grade and a pitch count on Mountain Project and nothing else — no start description, no landmark, no trip report. Its catalog approach paragraph is the North Ridge's boilerplate with a Forbidden West Ridge sentence left in it ('From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest'), which describes a different peak entirely. The North Ridge on the same formation IS written, and its baseFinding names the South Ridge as the undocumented side.
_SKIPPED.wa_goode_mountain_northeast_face: NO INDEPENDENT BASE IS PUBLISHED, AND THE ROW'S OWN BETA APPEARS TO BE THE NORTHEAST BUTTRESS'S. Every source found either merges this line with the Southwest Couloir and Black Tooth Notch, or does not describe it at all; no account gives a moat or bergschrund crossing specific to a true northeast-face-from-the-glacier line. Meanwhile the row's beta reads 'Grade IV 5.5 alpine rock with 6-8 pitches of low 5th class' — which is the Northeast Buttress's grade and character, not a spring snow-and-ice route, and its own season field says Apr-May. Writing a base here would mean either inventing one or copying the Buttress's red ledges onto a different line. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_storm_king_north_face: NOTHING TO RE-HOME. The row holds a name, an aspect, a first ascent (Emerson and Grove, 1978) and a gain figure, and its own beta says in as many words that it is documented only in brief first-ascent form with no pitch-by-pitch description, grade or length. Independent searching found exactly one titled trip report, which could not be retrieved, and every other North Face / North Ridge result resolved to a DIFFERENT Storm King — Colorado's San Juans, New York's Hudson Highlands, or Mount Storm King in the Olympics. Fabricating a start feature here is exactly how a foreign route gets onto a Washington peak.
_SKIPPED.wa_magic_mountain_southwest_cirque: THERE IS NO LINE TO FIND.
